和 FARMA2025），在标准化条件下系统比较三种对接程序（DOCK6、Vina、AD4）在四种任务（PR、CD、DE、RD）上的表现，并分析蛋白类别、配体性质、参数设置等因素对结果的影响。 2) 核心洞察 测试集构成决定评估结论 ：不同测试集（SB2025 vs FARMA2025 vs Astex2007）得出的程序性能排名不同，说明基准测试结果高度依赖测试集选择。FARMA2025 因更贴近真实药物发现场景，其评估结果对实际应用更具参考价值。 程序性能具有任务和类别依赖性 ：没有单一程序在所有任务和所有蛋白类别上表现最佳。DOCK6 在 PR 上略优，AD4 在 CD 矩阵成功率上最高，Vina 在 DE 上表现突出。这种差异源于各程序采样算法和打分函数的设计哲学不同。 参数设置比程序选择更重要 ：对于同一程序，box size 和 exhaustiveness 等参数对结果的影响可能大于程序间的差异。DOCK6 使用大 box 效果更好，而 Vina 和 AD4 使用小 box 效果更好，这与各程序的采样机制有关。 结构水对 CD 至关重要 ：HSP90 案例表明，包含结构水可显著提高 Vina 的 CD 成功率（从 19.7% 到 90.3%），说明在真实应用中考虑结构水的重要性。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] 基准测试设计应反映目标应用场景 ：如果目标是药物发现，测试集应包含已批准药物-靶标复合物，而非仅使用工具化合物。这一原则可迁移到其他计算方法的评估中（如 MD 模拟、AlphaFold 结构预测的评估）。 多维度评估优于单一指标 ：PR 精度高不代表 DE 或 RD 表现好，反之亦然。评估计算方法时应同时考察多个维度的性能指标。 「计算就绪」是基准测试可用的关键 ：提供标准化输入文件（mol2、pdbqt、grid 等）和脚本，降低用户使用门槛，是基准测试集被广泛采用的重要因素。 07 方法总览 输入 ： - 从 PDB 获取的蛋白质-配体复合物结构（1,244 个，分辨率 < 3.5 Å，平均 2.1 Å） - 配体三维结构及文献报道的质子化状态 - 蛋白质序列信息（UniProt 登录号）用于分类 输出 ： - SB2025 和 FARMA2025 测试集（含 DOCK6、Vina、AD4 三种格式的输入文件） - 四种任务（PR、CD、DE、RD）的定量评估结果 - 不同蛋白类别、配体性质、参数条件下的性能对比 模块 ： 1. 测试集构建模块 ：PDB 筛选 → 结构质量评估 → 配体质子化状态确定 → 蛋白质分类 → 文件格式转换 2. PR 评估模块 ：将配体从共晶结构中提取后重新对接，计算 RMSD 3. CD 评估模块 ：将同一蛋白家族的配体交叉对接至不同蛋白结构 4. DE 评估模块 ：将活性分子与诱饵分子混合对接，评估富集能力 5. RD 评估模块 ：将药物对接至 FARMA2025 中所有蛋白，评估靶标识别能力 工具 ： - DOCK6.12（含新加入的 simplex ramping 特征） - AutoDock Vina 1.1.2 - AutoDock 4.2.6（LGA 算法） - OpenBabel 2.4.1（格式转换） - AMBER（能量最小化） - AM1-BCC / Gasteiger 电荷模型 流程 （文字描述）： 1. 从 PDB 收集复合物结构，按标准筛选（分辨率、配体性质、非共价结合等） 2. 对每个复合物进行结构准备：加氢、分配质子化状态、能量最小化 3. 为三种程序分别准备输入文件（DOCK6: mol2 + grid；Vina: pdbqt；AD4: pdbqt + gpf） 4. 运行 PR 实验：每种程序使用其推荐参数进行对接，计算 RMSD 5. 运行 CD 实验：对 11 个蛋白家族进行交叉对接 6. 运行 DE 实验：使用 DUD-E 的 active/decoy 集合 7. 运行 RD 实验：将 FARMA2025 中 165 个药物对接至所有蛋白 8. 统计分析：按蛋白类别、配体性质、参数设置等维度比较三种程序 假设 ： - 共晶配体的结合模式代表真实结合模式（PR 评估的前提） - DUD-E 的 decoy 分子与 active 分子性质匹配但无活性（DE 评估的前提） - 药物与其共晶蛋白的结合亲和力高于与其他蛋白的结合（RD 评估的前提） 08 核心模块拆解 模块 功能 为何需要 输入输出 支撑证据 移除后的已知或预期影响 SB2025 测试集构建 提供大规模、多样化的对接评估平台 小规模测试集统计功效不足，无法覆盖多种蛋白类别 输入：PDB 复合物；输出：1,244 个计算就绪复合物 Results 表 1：SB2025 覆盖 17 个蛋白类别，322 个独特蛋白 移除后无法进行跨类别的系统比较 FARMA2025 药物子集 提供药物相关、无偏的评估子集 已批准药物与其靶标的复合物更能反映真实药物发现场景 输入：SB2025 中已批准药物复合物；输出：165 个药物-靶标复合物 Results 图 2：FARMA2025 与 FDA 2023 靶标分布 R²=0.72 移除后无法评估程序在药物相关场景中的表现 PR 评估协议 评估程序重现共晶结合模式的能力 PR 是对接程序最基本的性能指标 输入：复合物结构；输出：RMSD 分布、成功率 Results 图 3-4：三种程序 PR 成功率对比 移除后无法评估基本对接精度 CD 评估协议 评估程序在非共晶蛋白结构上的对接能力 真实应用中常需对接至同源或构象变化的结构 输入：11 个蛋白家族的复合物集合；输出：CD 矩阵、成功率 Results 图 5-6、表 3：CD 矩阵热图 移除后无法评估程序对蛋白构象变化的鲁棒性 DE 评估协议 评估程序区分 active/decoy 的能力 DE 是虚拟筛选的核心指标 输入：DUD-E active/decoy 集合；输出：ROC 曲线、AUC、富集因子 Results 图 7-8、表 4：AUC@1%FPR 对比 移除后无法评估程序的筛选能力 RD 评估协议 评估程序识别药物靶标的能力 RD 可用于药物重定位和靶标识别 输入：FARMA2025 中药物和蛋白；输出：靶标排名 Results 图 9-10、表 5：靶标排名统计 移除后无法评估程序的靶标识别能力 参数优化模块 确定每种程序的最佳参数组合 参数设置对结果影响大，需系统比较 输入：不同 box size、exhaustiveness、电荷模型；输出：最优参数组合 Results 表 2、图 3：参数对 PR 成功率的影响 移除后无法提供参数选择建议 结构水处理模块 评估结构水对 CD 的影响 HSP90 案例表明结构水对对接结果有显著影响 输入：含/不含结构水的 HSP90 体系；输出：CD 成功率对比 Results 图 6：HSP90 含/不含水 CD 结果 移除后无法提供结构水处理建议 09 关键公式符号 1. RMSD 计算（三种变体） ： - RMSDs （标准重原子 RMSD，基于原子顺序匹配）： [ RMSD_s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} | \mathbf{p}_i - \mathbf{q}_i |^2} ] 其中 ( \mathbf{p}_i ) 和 ( \mathbf{q}_i ) 分别为预测位姿和实验位姿中第 ( i ) 个重原子的坐标，( N ) 为重原子数。 RMSDh （对称性校正 RMSD，使用匈牙利算法进行原子匹配）： [ RMSD_h = \min_{\sigma \in S_N} \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} | \mathbf{p} i - \mathbf{q} {\sigma(i)} |^2} ] 其中 ( S_N ) 为所有可能的原子排列，匈牙利算法用于高效求解最小权重匹配。 RMSDm （最小 RMSD，基于 Trott 等人的方法）： [ RMSD_m = \min_{\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{t}} \sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} | \mathbf{R}\mathbf{p}_i + \mathbf{t} - \mathbf{q}_i |^2} ] 其中 ( \mathbf{R} ) 为旋转矩阵，( \mathbf{t} ) 为平移向量，允许在最小化 RMSD 的同时进行刚体变换。 2. 过表达/欠表达比例（Over/Under-Representation） ： [ \text{Over/UnderRepresentation} = 100 \times \left( \frac{\% \text{ProteinClass} {\text{Testset}}}{\% \text{ProteinClass} {\text{FDA2023}}} - 1 \right) ] 正值表示测试集中该蛋白类别相对于 FDA 2023 靶标分布过表达，负值表示欠表达。 3. 累积百分比差异（Cumulative % Difference） ： [ \text{Cumulative \% Diff} = \sum_{\text{classes}} \left| \% \text{ProteinClass} {\text{Testset}} - \% \text{ProteinClass} {\text{FDA2023}} \right| ] 用于量化测试集与 FDA 2023 靶标分布的整体差异，值越小表示测试集越能代表真实药物靶标分布。 4. 富集因子（Enrichment Factor, EF） （隐含于 DE 分析中）： [ EF_{1\%} = \frac{\text{Active hits in top 1\% of database} / \text{Total actives}}{\text{1\% of database} / \text{Total database}} ] 用于评估程序在数据库前 1% 中富集活性分子的能力。 10 实验设计与证据链 数据集/群体 ： - SB2025：1,244 个蛋白质-配体复合物，322 个独特蛋白，17 个主要蛋白类别 - experiments Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript presents a substantial and potentially valuable contribution to the computational drug discovery field through the introduction of two new benchmark datasets and a systematic comparison of three widely used docking programs. The work addresses an important need for standardized, clinically relevant test sets and provides a comprehensive evaluation framework. However, the current manuscript has several significant issues that need to be addressed, particularly regarding the clarity of the dataset construction methodology, the statistical rigor of the comparisons, and the interpretation of the reverse docking results. The claims about FARMA2025 being the first of its kind and the generalizability of the findings require more careful support. The manuscript would benefit from clearer presentation of the benchmarking protocols and more nuanced discussion of the limitations. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational chemists and structural biologists developing or using docking software would be the primary audience. Drug discovery researchers in both academic and industrial settings would find the benchmark datasets and comparative performance data valuable for tool selection and protocol optimization. The FARMA2025 dataset, in particular, would be of interest to those working on drug repurposing and target identification. The methodological framework for benchmarking could also inform future software development efforts. Major strengths 1. Introduction of two new benchmark datasets (SB2025 and FARMA2025) that address gaps in existing test sets, particularly the focus on approved drugs and the alignment with FDA drug target class distributions 2. Comprehensive benchmarking across four distinct tasks (PR, CD, DE, RD) under standardized conditions 3. Systematic exploration of key parameters affecting docking outcomes (sampling space, exhaustiveness, charge models, RMSD calculation methods) 4. The FARMA2025 dataset's design to mirror FDA drug target class distributions is a thoughtful approach to creating a clinically relevant benchmark 5. The authors' willingness to identify weaknesses in their own software (DOCK6) and explore parameter space is commendable Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodology clarity and reproducibility Claim pointer The manuscript claims to introduce "a calculation-ready set of 1,244 protein-ligand complexes" and that these are "freely available" for download Evidence pointer Methods section, "SB2025 Test Set Criteria" and "File Preparation for Energy Minimization and Docking" sections; location not provided Concern The description of how the SB2025 dataset was constructed is insufficiently detailed. While the authors mention criteria for inclusion (resolution, non-covalent binding, etc.), the specific workflow for how structures were selected, processed, and validated is not fully described. The claim that the dataset is "calculation-ready" requires a clear description of the exact preparation pipeline, including protonation state assignment, charge calculation methods, and any manual curation steps. Without this detail, other researchers cannot reproduce the dataset construction or fully understand potential biases in the benchmark. Why it matters The value of a benchmark dataset depends entirely on its construction methodology. If the preparation pipeline is not fully specified, users cannot assess whether the dataset is appropriate for their specific applications, and the reproducibility of the benchmarking results is compromised. This is particularly important given the authors' claim that this dataset improves upon previous versions. Resolution test The authors should provide a complete, step-by-step description of the dataset construction pipeline, including all software tools, parameters, and decision criteria used. Ideally, this would include a flowchart or pseudocode of the preparation process, and the exact commands or scripts used should be made available. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Statistical rigor of comparisons Claim pointer The manuscript states that "Averaged PR success rate across triplicate runs for DOCK6 was slightly improved compared to Vina (followed by AD4)" and makes similar comparative claims for CD, DE, and RD Evidence pointer Results sections for PR, CD, DE, and RD; location not provided Concern The statistical analysis of the differences between programs appears to be limited to reporting means and standard deviations. The manuscript does not describe any formal statistical testing (e.g., paired t-tests, Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, or ANOVA) to determine whether the observed differences between programs are statistically significant. Given the relatively small differences reported (e.g., 74.6% vs 71.0% for PR), it is unclear whether these differences are meaningful or within the range of random variation. Additionally, the manuscript does not discuss the distribution of results across the different protein families or ligand types, which could reveal important interaction effects. Why it matters The primary contribution of this work is the comparative benchmarking of three docking programs. Without proper statistical analysis, readers cannot determine whether the observed differences are robust or merely artifacts of the specific test set composition. This is particularly important for practical recommendations about which program to use for specific applications. Resolution test The authors should perform appropriate statistical tests to compare the performance of the three programs across all benchmarks. This should include both overall comparisons and analyses stratified by protein class or ligand properties. The results of these tests should be reported with appropriate effect sizes and confidence intervals. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Interpretation of reverse docking results Claim pointer The manuscript claims that "Challenging RD tests using FARMA2025, which gauge the ability to correctly rank the cognate structure best, indicate that generating the correct ligand pose is necessary but not sufficient" Evidence pointer Results section, "Reverse Docking (RD)" subsection; location not provided Concern The interpretation of the RD results as showing that "generating the correct ligand pose is necessary but not sufficient" is not well supported by the data presented. The manuscript reports CFR rates of 28.5% (DOCK6), 20.0% (Vina), and 10.9% (AD4), and PA-CFR rates of 91.5%, 90.9%, and 77.8% respectively. However, the relationship between pose accuracy and ranking accuracy is not systematically analyzed. The claim that pose accuracy is "necessary" would require demonstrating that cases where the correct pose is generated but the ranking is incorrect are systematically different from cases where both pose and ranking are correct. The current analysis does not provide this level of detail. Why it matters The RD results are presented as a key finding of the study, and the interpretation has implications for how researchers should approach target identification and drug repurposing studies. If the claim is not well supported, it could lead to incorrect conclusions about the utility of docking for these applications. Resolution test The authors should provide a more detailed analysis of the RD results, including a breakdown of cases where pose generation succeeded but ranking failed, and vice versa. They should also discuss potential reasons for these discrepancies and whether they relate to scoring function limitations or other factors. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generalizability of findings Claim pointer The manuscript states that "the PR studies suggest that DOCK6 performed best using a larger search space and AD4 performed best using a smaller search space" and makes similar generalizable claims about program performance Evidence pointer Results sections for PR and DE; location not provided Concern The benchmarking was performed using specific versions of each program (DOCK6.12, Vina 1.1.2, AD4.2.6) with specific parameter settings. The manuscript does not adequately discuss how these findings might generalize to other versions of these programs or to other docking software. Additionally, the choice of test set composition (e.g., the specific protein families and ligand types included) may limit the generalizability of the findings. The authors acknowledge this to some extent but do not provide a thorough discussion of the limitations. Why it matters Readers may be tempted to use these results to make decisions about which docking program to use for their specific applications. Without a clear discussion of the limitations and potential biases in the benchmarking, these decisions may be based on incomplete information. Resolution test The authors should include a more detailed discussion of the limitations of their benchmarking approach, including how the specific program versions, parameter settings, and test set composition might affect the generalizability of their findings. They should also discuss how their results compare to other published benchmarking studies. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Novelty and significance of FARMA2025 Claim pointer The manuscript claims that FARMA2025 "closely mirrors the distribution of FDA drug target classes for small molecules through 2023 (r² = 0.72)" and implies this is a novel contribution Evidence pointer Abstract and Results section, "Test Set Protein Class Composition" subsection; location not provided Concern While the concept of a drug-focused benchmark dataset is valuable, the manuscript does not adequately demonstrate the novelty of FARMA2025 compared to existing drug-focused benchmark sets. The authors mention that FARMA2025 is "the first of its kind" but do not provide a comprehensive comparison with other available drug-focused test sets. Additionally, the r² value of 0.72, while indicating a reasonable correlation, also indicates that 28% of the variance is unexplained, which could represent significant biases in the dataset composition. Why it matters The claim of novelty is important for establishing the significance of this contribution. If similar datasets already exist, the value of FARMA2025 is diminished. Additionally, understanding the limitations of the dataset composition is crucial for appropriate use. Resolution test The authors should provide a more comprehensive comparison of FARMA2025 with existing benchmark datasets, including a discussion of what makes it unique. They should also discuss the implications of the r² value and any potential biases in the dataset composition. ProteinMPNN，并整合结构幻觉实现闭环 de novo 发现，在 NK3R 上获得实验验证的功能活性候选多肽。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：如何为线性及环状多肽结合物设计高亲和力、结构稳定的氨基酸序列，使其在受体微环境中呈现生物活性构象？ 为什么重要 ：多肽治疗药物介于小分子和生物制剂之间，具有高特异性、低毒性等优势，但序列设计受限于受体口袋的物理化学约束，现有方法难以捕捉这些约束。 现有方法为何不足 ：当前计算方法（如 ProteinMPNN）将多肽设计视为通用逆折叠问题，仅依赖 backbone 几何，忽略受体口袋的详细物理化学环境（如残基侧链、氢键网络、疏水相互作用等），导致设计序列在界面适应性上欠佳。 精确研究问题 ：Can an all-atom receptor-aware geometric graph neural network outperform backbone-only inverse folding models in designing linear and macrocyclic peptide binders with improved sequence recovery, structural fidelity, and interface-level biophysical metrics? 04 背景与发展脉络 backbone 一起构建图结构，进行序列设计。 2) 核心洞察 受体不是背景，而是序列设计的「条件」 。多肽结合物的序列设计不应是「给定 backbone 预测序列」的通用逆折叠，而应是「给定受体环境预测能与之互补的序列」的受体条件化任务。全原子受体上下文提供了 backbone 几何无法捕捉的物理化学约束（如侧链相互作用、氢键供体/受体位置、疏水口袋形状等），这些约束直接决定多肽的界面适应性。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] 在分子设计中，「上下文」的粒度决定模型的信息上限。从 backbone-only 到 all-atom 的升级，本质上是将「几何约束」扩展为「物理化学约束」。 闭环设计（生成→筛选→实验验证）是深度学习分子设计的可行范式，但需要模型具备足够的初始精度才能让闭环收敛。 环状多肽的设计挑战可能源于其构象自由度受限，对序列-结构映射的精度要求更高，这为评估模型能力提供了更严格的测试场景。 07 方法总览 输入 ：受体全原子结构（PDB 格式）+ 多肽 backbone 坐标（或初始骨架） 输出 ：多肽氨基酸序列（线性或环状） 核心模块 ： 1. 图构建：将受体原子和多肽残基构建为几何图，节点为原子或残基，边基于空间距离 2. 同源建模假设模板与目标序列有足够同源性 端到端状态 ：GDEE 是 计算筛选平台 ，输出的是「优先实验验证的候选列表」，而非最终验证的酶变体。所有预测需经实验确认。 精度边界 ： - 最佳场景（X-ray 结构 + Rf-Score v2）：72% 正确率 - 完整流水线（建模 + 对接 + 打分）：约 54% 正确率 - 作者明确表示「不应被解释为支持对单个突变的二元成功/失败预测」 算力成本 ：文中未提供具体运行时间数据（Not assessable）。平台支持 MPI 并行，暗示为计算密集型工作流。 历史数据依赖 ：ML 打分函数训练于 PDBBind（实验结构），在预测结构上存在分布偏移，性能下降。 模型依赖 ：平台依赖 Modeller（同源建模）、AutoDock Vina/Smina（对接）、7 种 ML 打分函数——每个步骤的精度限制都会传播到最终结果。 最难情形 ：单点突变引起的 ΔΔG 变化通常很小，落在打分函数误差范围内；同源建模引入的结构偏差进一步降低信噪比。 群体/领域边界 ：评估数据集为 PDBBind（通用蛋白-配体复合物）和平台内部基准（260 对突变体），未在特定酶家族或工业相关酶上验证。 收尾 ：GDEE 是一个实用的自动化筛选平台，其价值在于 高通量初步筛选 和 减少实验候选数量 ，而非精确预测单个突变的效应。最佳使用方式是结合生化知识和活性位点检查，将计算排序作为实验设计的辅助工具。 12 作者自认局限 局限 具体表现 作者提出的未来方向 来源 结合亲和力 ≠ 催化效率 平台预测的是结合亲和力，而非 kcat/KM；结合改善不一定意味着催化改善 未明确提及（隐含：需结合其他方法预测催化） Introduction：binding affinity「does not ：作者区分了「独立基准」（PDBBind，测打分函数本身）和「端到端评估」（完整流水线，测系统性能），并明确归因性能下降于上游误差传播。这种分层评估设计值得在计算平台类工作中推广。 堆叠集成的条件性优势 ：集成模型在理想条件下最优，但在实际流水线中优势减弱——说明「模型集成」不能解决「上游数据质量」问题。这提示在构建端到端系统时，应优先改进上游步骤（如同源建模精度）而非堆叠更多下游模型。 可迁移方法 同源建模 + 多模型生成 + 质量筛选 ：每个变体生成多个模型（默认 5 个），用 VoroMQA 和 DOPE 评分筛选，只保留高质量模型进入对接。这一「生成-筛选」策略可迁移到任何基于结构预测的突变体评估任务。 距离约束过滤催化相关姿态 ：通过计算配体与特定残基（催化残基）的距离来过滤对接姿态，确保只考虑催化相关的结合模式。这一方法可迁移到酶工程中的底物特异性预测。 SQLite 全流程数据持久化 ：所有中间数据（序列、模型、姿态、打分）存储在 SQLite 数据库中，便于事后分析和调试。这种数据管理方式值得在计算平台中借鉴。 MPI 并行化 ：通过 MPI4Py 实现数据并行，支持大规模突变体库的分布式计算。对于计算密集型流水线，并行化设计是必要的工程实践。 对蛋白质结构计算研究的启示 ML 打分函数的分布偏移问题 ：ML 打分函数在实验结构上训练，在预测结构上性能下降——这提示在将 ML 模型应用于结构预测下游任务时，需要考虑训练-应用分布差异，可能需要在预测结构数据上微调。 「结合亲和力」作为酶工程筛选指标的边界 ：对于本课题（蛋白质结构 × AI/物理模拟），本文提供了一个重要警示：结合亲和力改善 ≠ 催化效率改善。在设计基于结构的酶工程筛选流程时，应考虑结合其他指标（如过渡态稳定化、构象采样等）。 15 ：本文的核心假设（结合亲和力可代理催化效率）与酶催化中「过渡态稳定化」理论存在张力。在设计酶工程筛选时，应意识到这一假设的边界。 候选方向（未验证） 将 GDEE 的「对接 + ML 重打分」策略迁移至蛋白质-蛋白质相互作用（PPI）预测 在 GDEE 中引入构象系综（ensemble docking）以部分缓解刚性受体假设 开发针对酶工程场景微调的 ML 打分函数（在突变体数据上训练） 16 No figures, tables, or supplementary files were provided. Assessment boundary Technical soundness of the described platform, validity of benchmarking claims, and adequacy of evidence for stated conclusions. No assessment of code functionality or reproducibility beyond what is described in text. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present GDEE, an automated, modular Python platform for structure-based enzyme engineering and gene discovery. The platform integrates sequence generation, homology modeling (Modeller), docking (AutoDock Vina or Smina), and scoring, with optional machine learning-based re-scoring. The authors benchmark scoring functions on PDBBind v2020 and on 260 protein pairs, and report that a stacking ensemble metamodel outperforms individual scoring functions in affinity prediction, though its advantage diminishes within the full pipeline. The authors conclude that the most effective protocol is Vina for pose selection followed by ML re-scoring for affinity ranking. Visible evidence base Text descriptions of benchmarking procedures and results. Reference to Supporting Information Sections S1, S2, S3, S3.1, and Figures S5, S6, S16, S18. No actual data, figures, or tables were provided in the submitted material. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures, tables, and Supporting Information files. The manuscript references Figure 1 (platform architecture), Figure 2 (database schema), Figure 3 (scoring function success rates), Figure 4 (histograms and mutation analysis), Table 1 (metamodel weights), and multiple supplementary figures. None of these were available for review. The two published case studies referenced in the text were not provided. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a potentially useful and extensible platform for structure-based enzyme engineering. The modular architecture and the integration of established tools (Modeller, AutoDock Vina, Smina) are sensible. The benchmarking effort, particularly the evaluation of ML scoring functions within the full pipeline context, addresses an important gap in the literature. However, the core claims regarding the platform's utility and the superiority of the proposed re-scoring approach are not verifiable from the provided material, as all quantitative results are contained in inaccessible figures and supplementary files. The reported performance of the best scoring function in the full pipeline (approximately 54% correct sign prediction) is modest and the authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation. The manuscript would benefit from clearer articulation of the novelty relative to existing enzyme engineering platforms and from a more critical discussion of the proxy relationship between binding affinity and catalytic efficiency. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in enzyme engineering, protein engineering, and metabolic engineering who require accessible, automated tools for variant prioritization. Computational biologists developing or benchmarking scoring functions for protein-ligand interactions would also find the comparative evaluation of interest. The platform's modular design may appeal to groups seeking to integrate structure-based workflows into their own pipelines. Major strengths 1. The platform addresses a real bottleneck in enzyme engineering: the need for automated, high-throughput variant prioritization. 2. The modular, object-oriented architecture with MPI support for distributed computing is a practical design choice. 3. The benchmarking includes a realistic full-pipeline evaluation, not just isolated scoring function tests. 4. The authors are transparent about the limitations of binding affinity as a proxy for catalytic efficiency and about the modest performance in the full pipeline. 5. The integration of ML-based re-scoring as an optional, configurable step is a thoughtful addition. Major Concerns 1. The central quantitative claims are entirely unsupported in the provided material. All figures and tables are missing, making it impossible to assess the validity of the benchmarking results, the statistical significance of differences between scoring functions, or the claimed superiority of the metamodel. 2. The novelty of the platform relative to existing tools is not clearly established. The authors state that GDEE has been "developed for some years" and applied to published case studies, but the specific innovations or advantages over existing platforms are not articulated. 3. The relationship between the benchmarking results and the platform's practical utility is unclear. The reported 54% success rate in the full pipeline is barely above chance, and the authors do not provide a clear decision framework for how users should interpret and act on the platform's rankings. 4. The manuscript lacks a critical discussion of the assumptions underlying the platform, particularly the use of rigid-receptor docking and the proxy relationship between binding affinity and catalytic activity. 5. The description of the "gene discovery" mode is underdeveloped. The text mentions BLAST-based pre-selection but does not explain how the platform handles sequence diversity, phylogenetic relationships, or the risk of selecting orthologs with different catalytic mechanisms. Minor Comments 1. The abstract would benefit from a quantitative summary of the platform's performance. 2. The introduction could more explicitly position GDEE relative to other automated enzyme engineering platforms (e.g., Rosetta, PROSS, FuncLib). 3. The description of the "Vina error range" in the context of ΔΔG predictions is vague. The authors should specify what error range they refer to and how it was determined. 4. The statement that "binding affinity indicates how strongly an enzyme can bind to its target molecule" is trivially true but does not address the more relevant question of how binding affinity relates to catalytic efficiency for different types of reactions (e.g., substrate binding vs. product release). 5. The manuscript would benefit from a discussion of computational cost and runtime for typical use cases. 6. The authors mention "less successful outcomes" from case studies but do not describe what these were or what lessons were learned. 7. The conclusions section overstates the platform's capabilities relative to the evidence presented, particularly the claim that it can "rapidly identify and optimize enzyme variants" without quantitative evidence of speed or success rate. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established 1. All quantitative benchmarking results are inaccessible. The authors must provide the actual data, figures, and statistical analyses. 2. The claim that the metamodel "outperformed all individual scoring functions" requires statistical testing (e.g., confidence intervals or significance tests) that is not described. 3. The full-pipeline evaluation is based on homology models, but the authors do not describe how model quality varies across the 187 reference proteins or whether model quality correlates with scoring performance. 4. The authors do not describe how the 260 protein pairs were selected or whether they represent a diverse and unbiased sample. 5. The manuscript does not specify how the "success" criterion (correct sign of ΔΔG) accounts for the magnitude of the predicted effect. A method that correctly predicts a tiny positive ΔΔG is counted the same as one that correctly predicts a large positive ΔΔG. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: Moderate. The combination of existing tools into an automated pipeline is useful but not conceptually novel. The benchmarking of ML scoring functions within a full enzyme engineering pipeline is a valuable contribution. Scientific importance: Moderate. The platform addresses a practical need, but the modest performance in the full pipeline limits its immediate impact. Interdisciplinary readership: Limited. The manuscript is primarily of interest to computational enzymologists and protein engineers. Technical soundness: Not assessable from the provided material. The benchmarking methodology is described, but the results are not visible. Readability for nonspecialists: Acceptable. The text is generally clear, though some sections assume familiarity with docking and scoring terminology. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript describes a potentially useful platform, but the core quantitative claims cannot be evaluated without the missing figures, tables, and supplementary material. The authors should be invited to resubmit with the complete data and with additional analysis addressing the concerns above. 在非活性态稳定中起重要作用，提示离子可作为 GPCR 构象调节的「第四配体」。 - Gαq 结合通过约束 TM6 动力学来「选择」活性样构象，体现受体-转导蛋白的双向别构效应。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis]: - 对 GPCR 或其他构象动态蛋白， 单一静态结构不足以描述功能 ；能量景观视角可解释 biased signaling 等复杂现象。 - 集合变量的选择决定采样质量 ：本文基于 GPCR 保守激活机制（TM5/TM6/TM7 重排）选择 CV，而非任意几何量，是方法成功的关键。 - 计算-实验闭环 （模拟预测 → 突变验证）是建立机制可信度的有效范式，可迁移至其他蛋白系统的功能研究。 07 方法总览 输入 : 起始结构：VPX 结合 PAR1 晶体结构 (PDB: 3VW7, 中间态)、PAR1-Gαq-TRAP cryo-EM 结构 (PDB: 8XOR, 的完整折叠动力学、脂质环境异质性、以及 Gαq 之外转导蛋白（Gαi, Gα12/13, arrestin）的竞争性结合。 oracle/真值输入 : 使用实验结构 (3VW7, 8XOR) 和 AlphaFold2 模型作为参考；AlphaFold2 模型虽经 GPCRdb 验证，但仍是计算预测，可能引入非活性态偏差。 端到端状态 : 计算模拟 + 实验验证已形成闭环，但实验仅验证了 Gq 通路，未覆盖 PAR1 的其他信号通路（如 β-arrestin）。 算力成本 : 6 个系统 × 42 images × 30 swarms × 10 ps × 300 迭代 ≈ 22.7 μs 总采样时间（不含 tMD 和无偏 MD），属于中等规模增强采样计算。 历史数据依赖 : 依赖 GPCRdb 的 AlphaFold2 模型和已有实验结构；CV 选择基于 β2AR 的保守激活机制，可能不完全适用于 PAR1 特有构象。 模型依赖 : 力场 (charmm36m)、水模型 (TIP3P)、膜组成 (POPC) 均为简化；未包含胆固醇、PI(4,5)P2 等可能调节 GPCR 构象的脂质。 最难情形 : 中间态构象的精确自由能值、氯离子结合的自由能贡献、Gαq 结合引起的构象变化幅度。 群体/领域边界 : 结论限于 PAR1 在 POPC 膜、0.15 M NaCl、310.15 K 条件下的构象行为；外推至其他 GPCR 或体内环境需谨慎。 有边界的复述 : 在 POPC 膜环境中，PAR1 的 apo 状态具有内在多构象性；VPX 通过限制 TM5/TM6 重排和维持 KRIT-Cl⁻ 协调来稳定非活性态；tethered agonist 通过促进 TM6 位移和 ICL3 重组织来稳定活性态；Gαq 结合进一步约束 TM6 KRK 基序的协调与非活性态稳定相关，提示在 MD 模拟中应显式包含生理相关离子，而非仅用中和盐。可迁移至其他含正电荷簇的蛋白系统。 AlphaFold2 模型的合理使用 : 将 AF2 预测结构作为非活性参考态，但需通过 GPCRdb 等工具验证其激活状态分类。可迁移至其他缺乏实验非活性结构的蛋白系统。 Gαq 单体的计算可行性 : 使用核苷酸-free Gαq 单体（而非全异源三聚体）即可捕捉受体-转导蛋白界面的关键相互作用，大幅降低计算成本。可迁移至其他 GPCR-G 蛋白或 GPCR-arrestin 复合物研究。 多投影分析策略 : 将自由能景观投影到多个互补描述符（a100、Y-Y 距离、TM6 位移等），可揭示单一投影可能遗漏的构象子状态。可迁移至任何高维自由能景观分析。 15 与已有知识连接 相似方法 : Fleetwood et al. 在 discussion, conclusion, and methods sections. Supplementary figure and table references noted but not provided. Assessment boundary Scientific content, methodological soundness, validity of claims relative to presented evidence, and alignment with Nature-style criteria. No assessment of formatting, grammar, or editorial fit. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors employ enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics simulations (string method with swarms of trajectories) to characterize ligand-dependent conformational energy landscapes of PAR1 across five receptor states. They identify a continuous activation pathway linking extracellular ligand engagement to intracellular motifs, validate key predictions through alanine mutagenesis and Gq-CASE BRET assays, and propose that different ligands modulate PAR1 signaling by reshaping the conformational landscape and microswitch network. Visible evidence base Full text of abstract, introduction, results, discussion, conclusion, and methods. References to supplementary figures S1–S9 and tables S1–S4, but these materials were not provided for review. Missing materials affecting confidence Supplementary figures S1–S9, supplementary tables S1–S4, all primary figures referenced in the main text (Figures 1–5 and associated panels), simulation parameter files, force field validation data, and raw experimental data. The absence of these materials limits verification of quantitative claims, convergence assessments, and experimental reproducibility. Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript presents a comprehensive computational investigation of PAR1 conformational dynamics using an established enhanced-sampling technique. The integration of multiple ligand conditions, Gαq binding, and experimental validation is commendable and addresses an important gap in understanding PAR1 activation mechanisms. However, the absence of all primary figures and supplementary materials prevents verification of the central quantitative claims, convergence assessments, and the quality of the experimental validation. The manuscript shows promise but cannot be fully evaluated in its current form. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in GPCR structural biology, computational biophysics, and pharmacology would find this work relevant. The study addresses fundamental questions about ligand-dependent conformational selection and allosteric communication in GPCRs, with potential implications for structure-based drug design targeting PAR1. The methodological approach combining SMwST with experimental validation may also interest computational biologists developing enhanced-sampling protocols for membrane proteins. Major strengths The study addresses a significant and timely question regarding PAR1 activation mechanisms. The use of SMwST is appropriate for exploring conformational transitions in GPCRs. The inclusion of five receptor states allows systematic comparison of ligand effects. The integration of computational predictions with experimental mutagenesis and BRET assays provides a validation framework. The identification of a continuous activation pathway with specific structural motifs is mechanistically informative. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence completeness Claim pointer The manuscript claims that free-energy landscapes were computed for five receptor states and that these reveal ligand-dependent modulation of PAR1 activation. Evidence pointer Results sections "Ligand-Dependent Modulation of the PAR1 Activation Free-Energy Landscape" and "Free-Energy Analysis Reveals Ligand-Specific Modulation of PAR1 Activation Motifs"; all primary figures referenced but not provided Concern The central quantitative results of this study are presented in figures that were not included in the review materials. Without access to the free-energy landscapes, convergence plots, and structural overlays, it is impossible to assess whether the claims about ligand-dependent modulation are supported by the data. The manuscript text describes qualitative trends but the quantitative evidence base is absent. Why it matters The core scientific contribution of this work is the characterization of conformational energy landscapes. If these landscapes cannot be examined, the validity of the entire computational analysis is unverifiable. Resolution test Provide all primary figures with appropriate resolution and detail. Include convergence assessments for the SMwST simulations, error estimates for free-energy surfaces, and clear labeling of all states and conditions. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological validation Claim pointer The manuscript claims that the string method with swarms of trajectories was applied and that 300 iterations were sufficient to achieve convergence. Evidence pointer Methods section "String Method with Swarms of Trajectories (SMwST)"; Figure S3 referenced but not provided Concern The convergence of SMwST simulations is critical for the reliability of computed free-energy landscapes. The manuscript states that convergence was assessed via the Frobenius norm but provides no quantitative convergence data. The choice of 42 images, 30 swarm trajectories, and 10 ps swarm length requires justification relative to the system size and the timescales of PAR1 conformational changes. The supplementary figure showing convergence was not available for review. Why it matters Inadequate convergence would invalidate all free-energy calculations and the subsequent mechanistic interpretations. The methodological choices must be rigorously justified and demonstrated to be sufficient for this specific system. Resolution test Provide convergence plots showing the Frobenius norm as a function of iteration number for all six systems. Include analysis demonstrating that the chosen swarm length and number of trajectories are sufficient to sample the relevant conformational space. Justify the choice of 42 images and the equilibration protocol. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Experimental validation Claim pointer The manuscript claims that alanine mutagenesis and Gq-CASE BRET assays validate predicted roles of key residues in activation and G-protein coupling. Evidence pointer Results section "Experimental Validation of Computationally Identified PAR1 Activation and G-Protein Binding Sites"; Figures 4 and 5 referenced but not provided; Table S2 referenced but not provided Concern The experimental validation is presented as supporting the computational predictions, but the actual data are not available for review. The manuscript reports p-values and effect sizes in the text but the figures showing dose-response curves, BRET traces, and statistical comparisons are absent. The selection criteria for which residues to mutate are not fully justified, and the relationship between the computational predictions and the specific experimental outcomes cannot be evaluated. Why it matters The experimental validation is a key differentiator of this study from purely computational work. If the experimental data do not robustly support the computational predictions, the central claims of the manuscript are weakened. Resolution test Provide all experimental figures with complete dose-response curves, appropriate error bars, and statistical analysis. Justify the selection of mutated residues based on the computational predictions. Include raw data or clear representation of replicates. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Force field and system setup Claim pointer The manuscript claims that the CHARMM36m force field was used and that the systems were prepared following standard protocols. Evidence pointer Methods section "MD System Preparation and Equilibration"; Table S3 referenced but not provided Concern The choice of CHARMM36m is appropriate for membrane proteins, but the manuscript does not provide details on how the force field parameters for the ligand (vorapaxar) were validated. The CGenFF parameters for VPX require validation against quantum mechanical calculations or experimental data. The protonation state assignment for D1482.50 is mentioned but the rationale and validation are not fully described. The system composition details in Table S3 were not available. Why it matters Force field accuracy and correct system setup are fundamental to the reliability of all simulation results. Errors in ligand parameterization or protonation states could significantly affect the computed free-energy landscapes. Resolution test Provide validation of VPX parameters, including comparison with QM reference data if available. Justify the protonation state choice with pKa calculations or experimental evidence. Provide complete system composition details. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Collective variable selection Claim pointer The manuscript claims that five transmembrane helix distance metrics were used as collective variables and that these reliably distinguish active, intermediate, and inactive conformations. Evidence pointer Methods section "String Method with Swarms of Trajectories (SMwST)"; Table S1 referenced but not provided; Figure S2 referenced but not provided Concern The choice of collective variables is critical for the string method. The manuscript states that the CV set was previously derived for β2AR and applied here to PAR1, but the transferability of these CVs to PAR1 is not fully justified. The validation that these CVs distinguish PAR1 conformational states (Figure S2) was not available. The manuscript does not discuss whether these CVs capture all relevant slow degrees of freedom for PAR1 activation. Why it matters If the collective variables do not adequately describe the conformational landscape, the computed free-energy surfaces and transition pathways may be incomplete or misleading. Resolution test Provide the validation of CVs for PAR1, including the distribution of known structures in CV space. Discuss the completeness of the CV set and consider whether additional degrees of freedom may be relevant for PAR1 activation. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity of presentation Affected element Results section "Ligand-Dependent Modulation of the PAR1 Activation Free-Energy Landscape" Evidence pointer Main text, first results subsection Issue The description of the free-energy landscapes is qualitative and relies heavily on figure references. The text describes "broad ensembles," "restricted conformations," and "shifts in free energy" without providing numerical values or quantitative comparisons between conditions. Required correction Include quantitative descriptions of free-energy differences, barrier heights, and population shifts where possible. Consider adding a table summarizing key free-energy values for each condition. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Methodological detail Affected element Methods section "Targeted MD" Evidence pointer Main text, Targeted MD subsection Issue The description of the targeted MD protocol lacks specific parameters such as the pulling rate, force constant for the rmsd restraint, and the criteria for selecting initial conformations for the string. Required correction Provide complete parameters for the tMD simulations to enable reproducibility. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Statistical analysis Affected element Experimental validation section Evidence pointer Results section "Experimental Validation of Computationally Identified PAR1 Activation and G-Protein Binding Sites" Issue The manuscript reports p-values for comparisons between mutants and wild-type but does not describe the statistical test used or whether multiple comparison corrections were applied. Required correction Specify the statistical tests used, the number of independent experiments, and whether corrections for multiple comparisons were applied. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Discussion of limitations Affected element Conclusion section Evidence pointer Main text, Conclusion Issue The limitations of the study are discussed briefly but do not address the potential impact of the simplified Gαq model (nucleotide-free, monomeric) on the conclusions about transducer-dependent stabilization. Required correction Expand the discussion of limitations to include the potential effects of the simplified Gαq model and the absence of Gβγ subunits on the computed free-energy landscapes. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Methods section "Free-Energy Calculation" Evidence pointer Main text, Free-Energy Calculation subsection Issue The manuscript states that the Demystify software was used for PCA but does not provide a version number or citation. Similarly, the Python scripts for the string method are referenced via a GitHub link but no version or commit identifier is provided. Required correction Provide version numbers and persistent identifiers for all software used to ensure reproducibility. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (missing figures), R1-M2 (convergence evidence), R1-M3 (experimental data availability). These are blocking because the central claims of the manuscript cannot be verified without the primary evidence. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The application of SMwST to PAR1 with systematic comparison of five ligand states is a novel contribution. The identification of a continuous activation pathway with specific structural motifs extends previous structural studies. However, the methodological approach itself is established, and the novelty lies primarily in the system-specific findings. Scientific importance: Understanding ligand-dependent conformational selection in PAR1 has implications for GPCR biology and drug design. The potential to inform pathway-selective modulator design is significant. However, the importance is somewhat limited by the focus on a single receptor and the absence of broader comparative insights. Interdisciplinary readership: The work bridges computational biophysics, structural biology, and pharmacology. The findings would interest researchers across these fields. The experimental validation component enhances accessibility to experimentalists. Technical soundness: The methodological approach is appropriate, but the inability to verify convergence and the absence of primary data prevent full assessment. The experimental validation appears sound based on the text description but cannot be verified. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is generally well-written and accessible. The introduction provides appropriate context. However, the results section relies heavily on figure references and assumes familiarity with GPCR activation terminology. Some sections, particularly the description of the string method, may be challenging for nonspecialist readers. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The manuscript addresses an important question with an appropriate methodology and includes valuable experimental validation. However, the absence of all primary figures and supplementary materials prevents verification of the central claims. The authors should be given the opportunity to provide the missing evidence. If the figures and supplementary data support the text descriptions, this could be a valuable contribution to the field.

supplied material Shared manuscript claim summary The authors use multiscale molecular dynamics simulations (all-atom, HREMD, USMD, and Martini coarse-grained) to characterize the GTP-induced closed-to-open conformational transition of the bacterial dynamin-like protein (BDLP) from Nostoc punctiforme. They report that GTP binding lowers the free energy barrier for opening by approximately 7–7.5 kcal/mol (corresponding to a ~5 orders of magnitude acceleration), that the open monomer remains thermodynamically unfavored, and that dimerization and membrane binding act synergistically to stabilize a semiclosed intermediate. They further identify a salt-bridge network that mediates allosteric communication and propose a refined mechanochemical cycle for BDLP. Visible evidence base Text descriptions of results from MD, HREMD, USMD, and CG simulations; RMSF analysis; free energy surfaces; PMF profiles; DCC analysis; clustering; PCA; DSSP analysis; ConSurf and gmx_MMPBSA calculations. Figures and tables are referenced but not visible in the provided material. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures, tables, and supplementary information are referenced but not provided. This includes Figure 1 (structures, RMSF, angles), Figure 2 (free energy surfaces), Figure 3 (salt bridges, DCC), Figure 4 (PMF profiles), Figure 5 (CG simulation results), Figure 6 (mechanochemical cycle), Table 1 (simulation summary), and all supplementary figures (S1–S8). Without these, quantitative claims cannot be independently verified. Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript presents a comprehensive computational study of a biologically important conformational transition in a dynamin-like protein. The methodological approach is ambitious and appropriate, combining multiple simulation techniques to address a question that is difficult to tackle experimentally. The central claims—that GTP binding accelerates the closed-to-open transition by lowering a free energy barrier, and that dimerization plus membrane binding stabilize the open state—are plausible and mechanistically interesting. However, the manuscript as provided has several significant weaknesses. First, the key quantitative claims (barrier heights, acceleration factors, free energy differences) cannot be verified without the figures and tables. Second, the claim of a "5 orders of magnitude" acceleration is derived from an Arrhenius extrapolation that is highly sensitive to the pre-exponential factor and the accuracy of the PMF; this warrants more careful justification and sensitivity analysis. Third, the coarse-grained simulations are described only briefly, and the evidence that dimerization and membrane binding "synergistically" stabilize the open state is not presented in sufficient detail. Fourth, the evolutionary conservation analysis is mentioned but its connection to the functional conclusions is underdeveloped. Overall, the study has the potential to be a valuable contribution, but the current evidence base is insufficient to fully establish the claims. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in the dynamin/GTPase field, computational biophysicists studying conformational transitions and allostery, and structural biologists interested in membrane remodeling proteins. The work provides a detailed atomistic model of how nucleotide binding couples to large-scale conformational change, which is a general problem in mechanochemical enzymes. Major strengths The study addresses a significant and timely question using a multi-technique simulation strategy. The identification of specific salt bridges as allosteric switches is mechanistically concrete and testable. The attempt to connect monomeric conformational dynamics to the requirements for membrane binding and dimerization is biologically relevant. The authors are appropriately cautious in noting that the open monomer is not thermodynamically favored, which is an important insight. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The manuscript claims that GTP binding lowers the free energy barrier for the closed-to-open transition by approximately 7–7.5 kcal/mol, corresponding to a ~5 orders of magnitude acceleration. Evidence pointer Figure 4 (PMF profiles), Figure S8 (error estimates), Methods section "Weighted Histogram Analysis Method" Concern The quantitative values for the barrier heights and the derived acceleration factor are central to the paper's message, but the actual PMF profiles, error bars, and the method for extracting the barrier from the PMF are not visible in the provided material. The conversion of a free energy barrier to a timescale using the Arrhenius equation with a fixed pre-exponential factor of 10⁻¹² s is a very rough estimate. The uncertainty in this factor alone could span orders of magnitude. Furthermore, the PMF is computed along a single collective variable (d_GT), and it is not demonstrated that this is a sufficient reaction coordinate to capture the true transition mechanism. The manuscript should show the PMF, discuss convergence, and provide a sensitivity analysis of the timescale estimate to the chosen pre-exponential factor. Why it matters The "5 orders of magnitude" acceleration is a headline claim that is used to argue for the biological significance of GTP binding. If this number is not robust, the central thesis is weakened. Resolution test The authors should provide the PMF figures with error bars, demonstrate convergence of the USMD simulations, and show how the timescale estimate changes with different reasonable values of τ₀. They should also discuss the limitations of using a single collective variable. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The manuscript claims that "BDLP dimerization and membrane binding are necessary to initiate the stabilization of the open conformation" and that these factors act "synergistically." Evidence pointer Figure 5 (CG simulation results), Results section "Membrane Anchoring Delays But Does Not Prevent Partial BDLP Closure" Concern The evidence for this central claim is presented in a single paragraph describing coarse-grained simulations. The details of the CG simulations (system setup, membrane model, protein parameterization, simulation length, analysis) are not provided in the main text, and the results are not shown. The claim of "synergy" requires a quantitative comparison of the stabilizing effects of membrane binding alone, dimerization alone, and both together. Without seeing the data, it is impossible to assess whether the conclusion is supported. The statement that membrane anchoring "delays but does not prevent" closure is also vague; the timescales and extent of closure are not quantified. Why it matters This is a key biological conclusion of the paper, distinguishing it from studies that focus only on the monomeric transition. If the evidence is weak, the paper's contribution is substantially reduced. Resolution test The authors should provide the CG simulation data, including time series of relevant order parameters (e.g., d_GT, RMSD) for all seven systems, and a quantitative analysis of the free energy or stability of the open state under different conditions. The claim of synergy should be backed by a direct comparison of the relevant free energy differences. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Methodological rigor Claim pointer The manuscript states that "GTP binding accelerates the transition by 5 orders of magnitude through an allosteric mechanism" and describes the allosteric network involving salt bridges. Evidence pointer Results sections "GTP Binding Ignites Communication across BDLP's Structure" and "GTP Binding Halves the Energy Needed for the Closed-To-Open Transition"; Figure 3 (salt bridges, DCC) Concern The allosteric mechanism is inferred from salt-bridge occupancy changes and DCC analysis. While these are reasonable approaches, the causal link between the identified salt bridges and the barrier reduction is not established. The manuscript does not show whether mutating these residues (in silico) would abolish the GTP effect, nor does it provide a quantitative measure of allosteric coupling (e.g., mutual information or perturbation response). The DCC analysis is performed on 600 ns trajectories, which may not be sufficient to capture the relevant correlated motions, especially for a large-scale transition. Why it matters The claim of an "allosteric mechanism" is a strong statement. Without a more rigorous demonstration of causality, it remains a hypothesis. Resolution test The authors could perform additional simulations with mutated salt-bridge residues to test their functional importance, or use more advanced allostery analysis methods. At minimum, they should discuss the limitations of their inference. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility Claim pointer The manuscript claims to be "the first all-atom MD investigation of a full-length dynamin-like protein" and "the first to map the complete closed-open transition pathway of BDLP, and dynamins in general." Evidence pointer Introduction section Concern These novelty claims are strong and should be carefully substantiated. The authors cite previous work that used coarse-grained simulations, but it is not clear whether other all-atom studies of dynamin family members (even if not full-length) have addressed similar transitions. The claim of "first" is always risky and requires a thorough literature search. The provided reference list is not visible, so this cannot be checked. Why it matters If the novelty claim is overstated, it could undermine the credibility of the paper. Resolution test The authors should carefully rephrase these claims to be more specific and defensible, e.g., "to our knowledge, this is the first all-atom study of the full-length BDLP transition" and provide a more detailed comparison with prior work. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract, first sentence Issue The phrase "From Closed to Mighty" in the title is catchy but not informative. The abstract would benefit from a more explicit statement of the key quantitative findings. Required correction Consider revising the title to be more descriptive, and ensure the abstract includes the key numbers (e.g., barrier heights, timescales) if they are robust. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Methods Evidence pointer Methods section "Overview of the Simulations" Issue The methods state that "all fine details of the simulation settings are provided in the Supporting Information." For a computational study, it is essential that the main text includes enough detail for a knowledgeable reader to reproduce the simulations without accessing the SI. Key parameters such as the force field version, water model, salt concentration, and equilibration protocol should be stated. Required correction Move the most critical simulation parameters to the main text or a table. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Interpretation Affected element Results section "GTP Binding Halves the Energy Needed for the Closed-To-Open Transition" Evidence pointer Figure 4 Issue The statement that GTP "halves" the energy needed is a specific quantitative claim. It is unclear if this refers to the barrier height or the overall free energy difference. The text should be more precise. Required correction Clarify whether the 7–7.5 kcal/mol reduction refers to the barrier height (kinetic) or the stability of the open state (thermodynamic), and use consistent terminology. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Discussion Evidence pointer Discussion section Issue The discussion of the mechanochemical cycle (Figure 6) is brief. The authors mention steps 5 and 6 rely on "well-documented experimental literature," but do not provide specific citations or explain how their simulations inform these steps. Required correction Expand the discussion of the proposed cycle, and clearly distinguish between what is directly supported by their simulations and what is inferred from the literature. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Presentation Affected element Results section "Open BDLP is Highly Dynamic and Can Adopt Semiclosed and Wide-Open Conformations" Evidence pointer Figure 1 Issue The term "wide-open conformation" is introduced but not quantitatively defined. It would be helpful to provide a metric (e.g., d_GT or hinge angle value) that distinguishes "open" from "wide-open." Required correction Define the conformational states quantitatively. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (barrier height and acceleration factor not verifiable without figures and with questionable Arrhenius extrapolation), R1-M2 (evidence for synergistic stabilization by dimerization and membrane binding is not presented in sufficient detail), R1-M3 (causal link between salt-bridge changes and barrier reduction not established). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The study addresses a well-known problem (dynamin conformational change) but with a novel computational approach and a focus on the full-length protein. The identification of specific salt-bridge switches is a potentially original contribution. However, the novelty claims are somewhat overstated and need to be tempered. Scientific importance The dynamin family is of broad biological importance, and understanding the mechanochemical coupling is a significant question. The finding that the open monomer is unstable and requires dimerization/membrane binding for stabilization is an important conceptual point. Interdisciplinary readership The topic is of interest to structural biologists, biophysicists, and cell biologists. The writing is generally accessible, but the heavy reliance on simulation jargon and the lack of clear figures may limit accessibility. Technical soundness The simulation methodology is state-of-the-art and appropriate. However, the key quantitative claims are not fully supported by the presented evidence, and the Arrhenius extrapolation is a potential weakness. The convergence of the USPMF and the sufficiency of the reaction coordinate are not demonstrated. Readability for nonspecialists The abstract and introduction are readable, but the results section is dense and assumes significant background knowledge. The lack of visible figures makes it difficult to follow the narrative. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The study has the potential to be a valuable contribution, but the current evidence base is insufficient to fully establish the central claims. The authors must provide the missing figures and data, strengthen the analysis of the coarse-grained simulations, and temper the novelty claims. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that GTP binding accelerates the transition by "5 orders of magnitude" is not verifiable from the provided material and is highly sensitive to the Arrhenius pre-exponential factor. The claim that dimerization and membrane binding act "synergistically" to stabilize the open state is not supported by the presented evidence. The claim that the identified salt bridges are "allosteric switches" is a hypothesis that is not causally tested. The claim of being "the first" all-atom study of a full-length dynamin-like protein and "the first" to map the complete transition pathway is not verifiable without a full literature comparison. The statement that "GTP binding must chronologically precede membrane insertion" is a strong conclusion based on structural analysis of a single state; it is not clear that this is a general requirement.

The protocol is claimed to require limited user intervention, enable consistent and reproducible analyses across targets, and is validated on the serotonin transporter and cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1), recovering known cholesterol-binding regions and identifying a potential additional site in CB1. The protocol is also applied to the CB1 negative allosteric modulator Org27569 to demonstrate generality beyond sterols. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, simulation parameters, validation metrics, or comparative benchmarks are provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, methods section, all figures and tables, simulation setup details, validation datasets, statistical analyses, and any comparison against existing methods Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially useful computational protocol for mapping cholesterol-binding hot spots in membrane proteins. The methodological concept is reasonable and the choice of validation targets is sensible given prior literature. However, the abstract provides no quantitative evidence of performance, no details on how "recovery" of known sites was assessed, and no comparison against existing approaches. The claim of generality based on a single additional application to a small-molecule ligand is not sufficiently supported. The work may be of interest to the computational biophysics and membrane protein communities, but the case is not established from the abstract alone. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biophysicists and cheminformaticians working on membrane protein-lipid interactions would be the primary audience. Researchers studying cholesterol modulation of membrane proteins, particularly transporters and GPCRs, may find the protocol useful for generating hypotheses about interaction sites. Developers of automated analysis workflows for molecular dynamics simulations may also be interested in the methodological contribution. Major strengths The protocol addresses a real need for automated, reproducible identification of cholesterol-binding sites across multiple membrane protein systems. The dual analysis approach combining contact persistence and spatial density is conceptually sound. The emphasis on limited user intervention and cross-target consistency is a practical advantage. The validation on two distinct protein classes and the extension to a non-sterol ligand suggest potential breadth. full text, figures, tables, or supplementary materials Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report that micheliolide (MCL) covalently engages Cys367 in the STAT3 DNA-binding domain (DBD), a residue unique to STAT3 among STAT family members, and that this modification disrupts STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activity without prior inhibition of upstream JAK phosphorylation. Using covalent docking, R-group enumeration, and free-energy perturbation (FEP) calculations, the authors designed and synthesized MCL analogs with comparable antiproliferative potency but improved physicochemical properties. Microscale thermophoresis (MST) confirms C367-dependent binding; microsecond-scale molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and pair-interaction energy analyses identify electrostatic interactions with Lys365, Val366, and Ile368 as dominant. Compound 16 is proposed as a next-generation lead. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no experimental details, numerical data, structural figures, or statistical analyses provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, experimental methods, compound synthesis and characterization data, assay protocols, statistical analyses, MD simulation parameters, FEP calculation details, and any supplementary information Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially interesting strategy for targeting a previously considered "undruggable" site in STAT3, with a clear translational rationale linked to pancreatic cancer and the clinical-stage compound ACT001. However, the evidence base available for assessment is limited to the abstract, which contains several claims that cannot be verified or fully evaluated without the underlying data. The central mechanistic claim, that C367 covalent engagement by MCL leads to downstream inhibition of STAT3 phosphorylation and transcriptional activity independent of JAK blockade, is intriguing but requires rigorous experimental support. The computational design pipeline is described in outline only, and the key claim that FEP-guided optimization was validated lacks quantitative detail. The identification of compound 16 as a lead is stated without comparative data. Overall, the work is potentially significant but the case is not established from the abstract alone. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in cancer biology, particularly those studying STAT3 signaling and pancreatic cancer; medicinal chemists interested in covalent inhibitor design and targeting challenging protein surfaces; computational chemists working on free-energy perturbation methods for covalent ligand optimization; and drug discovery groups focused on transcription factor targets previously considered undruggable. Major strengths The targeting of a non-canonical, STAT3-specific cysteine in the DBD represents a conceptually novel approach that could address selectivity limitations of SH2-domain inhibitors. The integration of computational design (covalent docking, FEP) with experimental validation (MST, MD, antiproliferative assays) reflects a modern drug discovery workflow. The link to ACT001, a clinical-stage compound, provides translational relevance. The claim that STAT3 inhibition occurs independently of upstream JAK blockade, if substantiated, would support a direct-on-target mechanism. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Mechanistic claim Claim pointer "This specific modification disrupts STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activity prior to any detectable inhibition of upstream JAK phosphorylation, a finding that suggests that STAT3 inhibition is not primarily driven by upstream kinase blockade." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract states that C367 modification disrupts STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705 and nuclear translocation, but the mechanistic logic is unclear. Phosphorylation at Tyr705 is required for STAT3 dimerization and nuclear translocation; if C367 modification prevents Tyr705 phosphorylation, the downstream effects on nuclear translocation and transcriptional activity would be expected consequences. However, the abstract does not explain how a covalent modification in the DBD would mechanistically interfere with phosphorylation at Tyr705, which is located in the SH2 domain. The temporal claim ("prior to any detectable inhibition of upstream JAK phosphorylation") is presented without data on time courses or dose responses. Why it matters The central mechanistic claim of the paper rests on this causal chain. If the connection between C367 modification and Tyr705 phosphorylation is not mechanistically explained and experimentally supported, the conclusion that STAT3 inhibition is not driven by upstream kinase blockade is not established. This distinction is critical for differentiating the proposed mechanism from conventional JAK/STAT pathway inhibitors. Resolution test Provide time-course and dose-response data showing that C367 modification occurs before and independently of changes in JAK phosphorylation. Include mechanistic experiments, such as mutagenesis of C367 (e.g., C367S or C367A) to demonstrate loss of MCL effects on Tyr705 phosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activity. Clarify the structural or allosteric basis by which DBD modification affects SH2-domain phosphorylation. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Computational validation Claim pointer "Guided by covalent docking, R-group enumeration, and relative binding free-energy calculations via free-energy perturbation (FEP), we have designed and synthesized a series of MCL analogs... validates FEP-guided optimization of covalent inhibitors." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract claims that FEP-guided optimization was validated, but no quantitative correlation between computed and experimental values is provided. No binding free-energy values, rank-order comparisons, or experimental binding affinities are reported. The phrase "validates" is a strong claim that requires demonstration that FEP predictions accurately ranked compounds against experimental measurements (e.g., MST-derived Kd values or cellular potencies). Why it matters The methodological contribution of the paper, as stated, is the validation of FEP for covalent inhibitor optimization. Without quantitative agreement between predictions and experiments, the claim of validation is unsupported. This is a key differentiator for the paper's significance to the computational chemistry community. Resolution test Provide a scatter plot or table correlating computed relative binding free energies with experimentally determined binding affinities or potencies for the full series of synthesized analogs. Report statistical metrics (e.g., Pearson R, Kendall tau, mean unsigned error). If FEP was used only for ranking a subset, state this explicitly and provide the relevant comparisons. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Selectivity claim Claim pointer "Cys367 (C367)-dependent covalent engagement within the DNA-binding domain (DBD)-a residue unique to STAT3 among STAT family members." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract claims C367 is unique to STAT3 among STAT family members, but no sequence alignment or structural comparison is provided. The abstract also does not address potential off-target reactivity of the covalent warhead with other cysteine-containing proteins beyond the STAT family. Selectivity is claimed only in terms of STAT family uniqueness, not broader proteome-wide selectivity. Why it matters For a covalent inhibitor, selectivity is a primary concern. The claim of targeting a "unique" residue is necessary but not sufficient to establish selectivity. Without evidence of minimal off-target reactivity, the translational potential of compound 16 is not established. Resolution test Provide a sequence alignment of STAT family DBDs showing C367 is unique. Include a selectivity assay, such as a cysteine-reactive proteome profiling experiment (e.g., activity-based protein profiling with a clickable probe) or a panel of related transcription factors and kinases, to demonstrate that MCL and compound 16 do not broadly react with other cysteines. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Lead compound claim Claim pointer "Identifies compound 16 as a promising next-generation lead with a superior drug-like profile for targeting STAT3-dependent cancers." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern Compound 16 is named as a lead, but no comparative data are provided against MCL or other analogs. "Superior drug-like profile" is stated without quantitative metrics for solubility, lipophilicity, permeability, metabolic stability, or selectivity. No in vivo data are mentioned. Why it matters The designation of a lead compound requires evidence that it improves upon the parent compound in relevant properties while retaining efficacy. Without comparative data, the claim is not assessable. Resolution test Provide a table comparing compound 16 with MCL and other key analogs across the measured properties (kinetic solubility, logP or logD, permeability, metabolic stability, antiproliferative IC50, binding affinity). If in vivo data exist, include them; if not, state that the lead designation is based on in vitro properties only. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Mechanistic narrative Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract states that C367 modification disrupts Tyr705 phosphorylation, nuclear translocation, and transcriptional activity, but the order of these events and their causal relationships are not clearly articulated. The phrase "prior to any detectable inhibition of upstream JAK phosphorylation" is ambiguous regarding the time frame and the assay used. Required correction Clarify the temporal sequence of events with explicit time points and specify which JAK isoforms were assessed. State whether the effect on Tyr705 phosphorylation is direct (e.g., steric blockade of the kinase-substrate interaction) or indirect (e.g., conformational change). Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element "Undruggable" claim Evidence pointer Title; location not provided Issue The title uses "Undruggable" in quotes, which is appropriate, but the abstract does not define what makes the STAT3 DBD "undruggable" or how the current approach overcomes the specific challenges (e.g., lack of a deep binding pocket, protein-protein interaction surface). Required correction Briefly state the specific challenges of targeting the DBD and how covalent engagement of C367 addresses them. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Data reporting Affected element MD simulation claims Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract mentions "microsecond-scale molecular dynamics simulations and pair-interaction energy analyses" but provides no details on the number of replicates, force field, system setup, or convergence criteria. The claim that "electrostatic interactions predominate" is stated without quantitative energy values. Required correction Provide simulation details in the main text or methods, and report the pair-interaction energy values for the key residues (Lys365, Val366, Ile368) to support the claim. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Context Affected element Comparison to existing inhibitors Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract states that conventional SH2-domain inhibitors have "limited selectivity and efficacy" but does not cite specific examples or compare the current compounds to any known STAT3 inhibitors. Required correction Add a brief comparison to representative SH2-domain inhibitors (e.g., stattic, S3I-201) in terms of potency, selectivity, or physicochemical properties. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (mechanistic link between C367 modification and Tyr705 phosphorylation), R1-M2 (lack of quantitative FEP-experiment correlation), R1-M3 (insufficient selectivity evidence), R1-M4 (no comparative data for compound 16) Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The concept of targeting a STAT3-specific cysteine in the DBD with a covalent inhibitor derived from a clinical-stage natural product is original and potentially impactful. Scientific importance: If fully substantiated, the work could provide a new strategy for targeting STAT3 in cancers where current inhibitors have failed, with implications for pancreatic cancer therapy. Interdisciplinary readership: The work bridges cancer biology, medicinal chemistry, and computational chemistry, which could appeal to a broad audience, but the abstract is too specialized in its current form to engage nonspecialists. Technical soundness: Not assessable from the abstract alone; the computational and experimental methods are described only in outline, and key validation data are missing. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is dense and assumes familiarity with STAT3 biology, covalent inhibitor design, and FEP methodology; the mechanistic logic is not clearly explained for a general scientific audience. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract presents a plausible and interesting hypothesis with a reasonable experimental plan, but the central mechanistic claim, the validation of the computational approach, and the lead compound designation all require substantial additional evidence. A revised manuscript with full data would be needed to assess whether the claims are supported.

They introduce a Markov state model (MSM) based framework using radius of gyration and RMSD fluctuations to calculate binding free energy landscapes. They report that the D33K/E36K/E37K/E41K mutant most strongly destabilizes the complex, while the other two mutants behave closer to wild type. They compare MSM results with MM-PBSA calculations and prior experimental data, concluding that MSM yields more realistic binding free energies than MM-PBSA. Visible evidence base Abstract text only. No figures, tables, methods details, or numerical results are provided. Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, simulation protocols, force field parameters, convergence criteria, MSM construction details, MM-PBSA settings, error estimates, and the experimental reference data used for comparison Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a potentially useful computational framework for assessing mutation effects on protein-protein binding, and the biological question regarding Nsp1-NXF1-RRM interactions is relevant to SARS-CoV-2 host modulation. However, the abstract alone provides insufficient detail to evaluate the validity of the MSM-based free energy approach, the statistical robustness of the results, or the strength of the claimed agreement with experiment. The central methodological novelty, namely the use of radius of gyration and RMSD fluctuations as MSM collective variables for binding free energy estimation, is not adequately justified or benchmarked within the visible material. The claim that MSM yields "more realistic" values than MM-PBSA requires quantitative support that is not presented. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biophysicists and structural biologists studying protein-protein interactions, particularly those developing or applying enhanced sampling and Markov state model methodologies. Researchers working on SARS-CoV-2 host-pathogen interactions and viral immune evasion mechanisms would also find the biological context relevant. The methodological comparison between MSM and MM-PBSA may interest practitioners seeking more physically grounded free energy estimates for mutational scanning. Major strengths The study addresses a biologically important interaction with clear translational relevance. The use of multiple complementary approaches (structural analysis, energetic analysis, MSM, MM-PBSA) is methodologically sound in principle. The comparison with prior experimental work provides a benchmark for the computational predictions. The focus on mutation-induced changes rather than absolute binding affinities is a sensible framing that may reduce systematic error concerns. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological validity Claim pointer The authors claim that their MSM-based framework, using fluctuations of radius of gyration and RMSD from a reference state, can calculate the free energy landscape of protein-protein binding and yield "more realistic" binding free energy values than MM-PBSA. Evidence pointer Abstract, methods description (location not provided) Concern The abstract does not explain how a one-dimensional or low-dimensional projection onto radius of gyration and RMSD captures the relevant binding free energy surface. Protein-protein binding involves complex conformational rearrangements, desolvation, and entropic contributions that are unlikely to be fully described by these two collective variables. No validation against known binding free energies, no comparison with more rigorous methods (e.g., umbrella sampling, metadynamics, or free energy perturbation), and no convergence assessment are presented. Why it matters If the MSM collective variables do not adequately resolve the binding/unbinding transition states and metastable states, the resulting free energy estimates could be systematically biased. The claim of superiority over MM-PBSA rests entirely on this methodological foundation, which is not established from the abstract.
