(abstract, introduction, materials and methods, results, discussion, conclusion) without figures, tables, or supplementary material Assessment boundary Scientific soundness, internal consistency, and support of claims based solely on the provided text; no assessment of figures, tables, or supplementary data that were not supplied Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose that computational structure prediction (AlphaFold2, PSIPRED) and charge analysis can guide the selection of peptides for fusion to bacteriophage lysins to enhance activity against Gram-negative bacteria under physiological conditions. They report that α-helical, positively charged fused peptides correlate with improved bactericidal activity of engineered lysins in high NaCl and serum, based on screening seven LysPd138 variants and validating with two LysPd149 variants. Visible evidence base Text descriptions of experimental procedures and results; references to Figures 1–6, Supplementary Figures S1–S6, Supplementary Table S1; no actual data values, statistical outputs, or images were provided Missing materials affecting confidence All figures, tables, and supplementary material; raw CFU data; statistical analysis outputs; SDS-PAGE images; AlphaFold structure predictions; PSIPRED outputs; NPN uptake fluorescence values; peptide sequences and charge calculations Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a relevant problem in lysin engineering against Gram-negative bacteria and proposes a computationally informed selection strategy that could reduce trial-and-error screening. The core hypothesis, that α-helical propensity and positive charge of fused peptides correlate with enhanced activity under physiological conditions, is plausible and supported by the described pattern of results. However, the evidence base as presented is incomplete. The manuscript relies heavily on figures and supplementary data that were not provided for review, making it impossible to verify the reported outcomes, statistical claims, or structural predictions. The correlational nature of the findings is acknowledged by the authors, but the mechanistic interpretation remains speculative. The study is a proof-of-concept with limited generalizability, and several methodological details require clarification. The writing is generally clear, though some results are described with insufficient quantitative detail. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in antimicrobial drug development, bacteriophage biology, and protein engineering would find this work relevant. The proposed workflow combining structure prediction and charge analysis for peptide selection could be of practical interest to groups working on lysin therapeutics against Gram-negative pathogens, particularly Acinetobacter baumannii. The study also contributes to the growing literature on computational approaches to guide protein engineering. Major strengths Addresses a clinically relevant problem: loss of lysin activity against Gram-negative bacteria under physiological conditions. Proposes a rational, computationally informed strategy that could reduce the cost and labor of empirical screening. Includes a validation step using a second lysin (LysPd149), strengthening the generalizability of the observed correlation. Authors acknowledge limitations, including low pLDDT confidence scores and the correlational nature of the findings. Comparative assessment of engineered lysins versus free peptide in plasma provides useful translational information. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence completeness Claim pointer The authors claim that specific variants (Syn138, Pad138, CecA138) "eradicated the bacteria to below the detection limit" in 150 mM NaCl and sera, and that other variants "significantly lost their bactericidal effects." Evidence pointer Results section, Figures 2A, 2C, 2D, 3A, 3B, 3C; location not provided Concern The actual data supporting these claims are presented only in figures that were not supplied for review. No numerical CFU values, log reductions, or statistical test results are reported in the text. The reader cannot verify the magnitude of the reported effects, the variability between replicates, or whether the differences between active and inactive variants are statistically robust. The claim that certain variants "eradicated" bacteria to below detection limits requires confirmation of the detection limit of the assay and the consistency of this outcome across replicates. Why it matters The central conclusion of the manuscript, that α-helical positively charged peptides confer enhanced activity, rests entirely on the differential activity patterns of the variants. Without access to the underlying data, the validity of this conclusion cannot be assessed. The manuscript is not self-contained in its current form. Resolution test Provide the actual CFU data, log reduction values, and statistical comparisons for all variants under all tested conditions, either in the main text or as accessible supplementary data. Include detection limits and replicate numbers. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Structural evidence Claim pointer The authors claim that AlphaFold2 and PSIPRED predictions show that active variants are fused to peptides with predominantly α-helical structures, while inactive variants have loop-like structures. Evidence pointer Results section, Figures 2B, 2E, Supplementary Figures S2, S3, S4, S5; location not provided Concern The structural predictions are central to the manuscript's hypothesis, yet the actual prediction outputs are not shown in the provided text. The authors note that pLDDT scores for most fused peptide regions were below 50, indicating low confidence in the predicted structures. This is a significant caveat that undermines the reliability of the structural assignments. The agreement between AlphaFold2 and PSIPRED is mentioned but not demonstrated. For Buf149, the peptide is described as "partially α-helical" but this is not shown or quantified. Why it matters The manuscript proposes that structure prediction can guide peptide selection. If the predictions themselves are of low confidence, the practical utility of the approach is questionable. The authors need to demonstrate that the structural assignments are robust enough to be used as a screening criterion. Resolution test Show the predicted structures with confidence annotations, provide the PSIPRED secondary structure outputs for all seven peptides, and discuss how the low pLDLT scores were interpreted. If possible, provide experimental validation (e.g., circular dichroism) or at least a clear justification for relying on low-confidence predictions. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Mechanistic interpretation Claim pointer The authors suggest that the enhanced activity of α-helical positively charged peptide fusions is due to improved interaction with the negatively charged outer membrane, supported by NPN uptake assays. Evidence pointer Results section, Supplementary Figure S6; location not provided Concern The NPN uptake assay is presented as supporting the proposed mechanism, but the data are not shown. The authors report "2.6-, 2.3-, 2.8-, and 1-fold increases" in NPN uptake for specific variants, but the baseline, the statistical significance, and the comparison with native lysin are not described in the text. The correlation between NPN uptake and bactericidal activity is not quantitatively established. Why it matters The proposed mechanism linking α-helicity, charge, membrane permeabilization, and bactericidal activity is a key part of the manuscript's contribution. Without clear evidence for the membrane permeabilization step, the mechanistic claim remains speculative. Resolution test Provide the NPN uptake data with appropriate controls, statistical analysis, and a direct comparison between variants with high and low activity. Discuss whether the observed permeabilization is sufficient to explain the bactericidal effects. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generalizability Claim pointer The authors propose that their computational strategy could be broadly applicable to engineering lysins against Gram-negative bacteria, stating it "may improve the efficiency of lysin engineering." Evidence pointer Discussion section; location not provided Concern The study uses only two lysins (LysPd138 and LysPd149) and a single bacterial strain (A. baumannii WHH40137). The authors acknowledge this limitation, but the claim of broader applicability is not supported by the data. The correlation between α-helicity, charge, and activity may be specific to these lysins or this bacterial strain. Why it matters The practical value of the proposed strategy depends on its generalizability. If the correlation does not hold for other lysins or bacterial species, the approach would have limited utility. Resolution test Acknowledge more explicitly that the findings are preliminary and require validation across a broader panel of lysins and Gram-negative species. Alternatively, provide additional data from other lysin-peptide combinations if available. R1-M2: The structural predictions are based on low-confidence AlphaFold2 models, and the PSIPRED outputs are not shown. R1-M3: The NPN uptake data supporting the proposed mechanism are not presented. The manuscript relies on figures and supplementary material that were not supplied, making a full technical assessment impossible. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality Moderate. The application of AlphaFold2 and PSIPRED to guide peptide selection for lysin engineering is a reasonable extension of existing approaches, but the concept of using computational prediction to inform fusion design is not entirely novel. The specific focus on α-helicity and charge as predictive features is a useful contribution. Scientific importance Moderate. The problem of lysin activity against Gram-negative bacteria is important, and a rational design strategy would be valuable. However, the study is a proof-of-concept with limited data, and the clinical or practical impact is not yet demonstrated. Interdisciplinary readership Limited. The work is primarily of interest to researchers in antimicrobial development and protein engineering. It is unlikely to attract a broad interdisciplinary audience. Technical soundness Cannot be fully assessed. The described methods are generally appropriate, but the lack of accessible data and the low confidence of structural predictions raise concerns. The correlational design limits the strength of the conclusions. Readability for nonspecialists Adequate. The manuscript is generally well-written and explains the rationale clearly. However, some sections assume familiarity with lysin biology and structural prediction tools. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript presents an interesting hypothesis and a plausible workflow, but the evidence base is incomplete. The central claims cannot be verified without access to the figures and supplementary data. The low confidence of the structural predictions and the correlational nature of the findings further weaken the case. The authors should be encouraged to resubmit with full data availability and, ideally, experimental validation of the predicted structures. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that α-helical positively charged fused peptides are responsible for enhanced bactericidal activity is correlational and not causally established. The claim that the computational workflow can reduce time and cost of lysin engineering is speculative and not supported by any comparative analysis. The claim that mouse serum inhibits lysin activity more than human serum is reported without mechanistic explanation or supporting data in the text. The structural assignments of the fused peptides are based on low-confidence predictions and are not experimentally validated. The generalizability of the findings beyond the two lysins and one bacterial strain tested is not supported.

研究问题 具体问题 : 在鸭巴氏杆菌病（Pasteurella multocida 感染）中，线粒体编码基因（CytB、CytC）与核编码先天免疫基因（NLRP3、IL-18、STING）之间是否存在协同表达与蛋白互作，从而共同影响宿主抗细菌免疫？ 为什么重要 : 线粒体不仅是能量代谢中心，也是先天免疫信号枢纽（如 mtDNA 释放激活 cGAS-STING、NLRP3 炎症小体）。但线粒体-核互作在禽类细菌性疾病中的具体分子机制尚不清楚，且鸭作为重要经济禽类，其抗病遗传基础研究不足。 现有方法为何不足 : 已有研究多集中于哺乳动物（小鼠、人）的病毒或胞内菌感染模型，对禽类、胞外菌（P. multocida）以及线粒体编码蛋白与核免疫基因的直接互作缺乏系统研究；且多数研究仅关注单一通路，未将线粒体基因与核免疫基因放在同一互作网络中分析。 精确研究问题 : Can mitochondrial-encoded proteins (CytB, CytC) functionally interact with nuclear-encoded innate immune molecules (NLRP3, IL-18, STING) to coordinately regulate antibacterial immunity during P. multocida Visible evidence base Sequence characterization, in silico 3D modeling, molecular docking, differential mRNA expression profiling (qPCR), pathway enrichment analysis, and protein-protein interaction network analysis Missing materials affecting confidence Figures 1-14 referenced but not provided; supplementary material not provided; raw qPCR data not provided; statistical details (error bars, replicates, significance thresholds) not fully described; accession numbers for NLRP3 not provided; details of docking validation not provided Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript addresses an interesting and potentially important topic, namely the cross talk between mitochondrial and nuclear-encoded genes in antibacterial immunity. However, the study as presented is largely descriptive and correlative, and the central claim of functional interaction between mitochondrial and nuclear immune molecules is not experimentally tested. The evidence base consists primarily of in silico predictions and differential expression data, which are insufficient to establish the mechanistic conclusions drawn. The manuscript also contains significant structural and reporting issues, including duplicated text, incomplete methodological details, and overinterpretation of pathway analyses. The work may be of interest to researchers studying mitochondrial immunity or avian host-pathogen interactions, but in its current form the case is not established. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers studying mitochondrial biology in immunity, avian immunology, host-pathogen interactions, and innate immune signaling may find the descriptive data useful as a starting point. The duck model of pasteurellosis is of veterinary relevance, and the comparative expression data for NLRP3, IL-18, STING, and mitochondrial genes in infected versus healthy birds could inform future studies. However, the lack of functional validation limits the broader appeal. Major strengths The study addresses a timely and underexplored topic, namely mitochondrial-nuclear cross talk in antibacterial immunity. The use of a natural infection model in an indigenous duck breed is a practical and relevant approach. The combination of sequence characterization, structural prediction, and expression profiling provides a multi-angle descriptive dataset. The authors appropriately acknowledge limitations in interpreting cytochrome b expression as a proxy for mitochondrial copy number. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Experimental evidence for functional interaction Claim pointer The manuscript claims that mitochondrial-encoded proteins "functionally interact" with nuclear-encoded immune regulators (NLRP3, IL-18, STING) and that this interaction regulates antibacterial immunity. Evidence pointer Results section, Discussion section, Figures 9-14 Concern The central claim of functional interaction is not supported by any direct experimental evidence. The study relies on in silico docking, STRING interaction predictions, and KEGG pathway enrichment, none of which demonstrate actual physical or functional interaction in a biological system. No co-immunoprecipitation, pull-down, knockout, knockdown, overexpression, or reporter assays are presented. The differential expression data are correlative and do not establish causality or interaction. Why it matters The title and abstract promise a mechanistic insight into mitochondrial-nuclear cross talk in antibacterial immunity. Without functional validation, the claims are overstated and the scientific contribution is limited to descriptive observation. Resolution test Provide direct experimental evidence of interaction, such as co-immunoprecipitation of cytochrome b/cytochrome c with NLRP3, IL-18, or STING in duck cells; or demonstrate that manipulation of mitochondrial gene expression alters nuclear immune gene expression and antibacterial outcomes. Alternatively, substantially revise the claims to reflect the descriptive nature of the findings. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Statistical rigor and data presentation Claim pointer The manuscript reports "significantly higher expression" of cytochrome b, cytochrome c, NLRP3, IL-18, and STING in healthy ducks compared to infected ducks. Evidence pointer Results section, Figures 6-7, Statistical analysis subsection Concern The statistical analysis is inadequately described. The authors state that "Microsoft Excel was used for descriptive statistical analysis" and that "Statistical analyses were performed using SYSTAT version 13.1," but no specific tests, significance thresholds, or correction for multiple comparisons are reported. The figures are not provided, so it is impossible to assess variance, effect sizes, or whether assumptions for the chosen tests were met. The sample size (n=6 per group) is small, and no power analysis is presented. Why it matters The differential expression data are the only experimental results in the study. Without rigorous statistical reporting, the conclusions drawn from these data cannot be evaluated or reproduced. Resolution test Provide full statistical details, including the specific tests used, exact p-values or confidence intervals, effect sizes, and information on data distribution and variance. Include raw data or accessible supplementary tables. Ensure figures show individual data points, error bars, and significance indicators. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological completeness and reproducibility Claim pointer The methods describe sequence characterization, 3D modeling, docking, and expression profiling, but key details are missing. Evidence pointer Materials and Methods section, Tables 1-3 Concern Several methodological details are missing or incomplete. The authors do not specify the reference sequences used for primer design for all genes, the efficiency of qPCR primers, the normalization strategy beyond GAPDH, or whether multiple reference genes were evaluated. The docking methodology is described only as "PatchDock algorithm" with no mention of input structure preparation, scoring function details, or validation of docking results. The criteria for selecting "putative interaction sites" are not defined. The authors also do not state how many biological and technical replicates were used for qPCR. Why it matters Reproducibility is a core requirement for scientific publication. The current level of methodological detail is insufficient for other laboratories to replicate the experiments or for reviewers to assess the validity of the approaches. Resolution test Provide complete methodological details, including primer sequences with GenBank accession numbers for all target genes, qPCR cycling conditions, melting curve analysis, primer efficiency data, normalization strategy, and statistical treatment. For docking, specify the structures used, preparation steps, scoring functions, and any validation (e.g., re-docking of known complexes). Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Interpretation of pathway and interaction analyses Claim pointer The manuscript states that KEGG pathway analysis identified involvement of NOD-like receptor signaling, cytosolic DNA sensing, phagocytic pathways, and necroptosis, and that STRING analysis revealed "extensive protein-protein interaction networks." Evidence pointer Results section, Figures 10-14 Concern The pathway and interaction analyses are overinterpreted. The authors appear to have performed KEGG enrichment on a very small set of genes (five total), which is statistically underpowered and unlikely to yield meaningful enrichment. The STRING analysis is based on predicted interactions, not experimental evidence, and the confidence scores are not reported. The claim that these analyses "support a model" of coordinated interaction is not justified by the data. Why it matters Overinterpretation of in silico predictions as biological evidence can mislead readers and inflate the perceived significance of the findings. Resolution test Either remove or substantially temper the pathway and interaction claims. If these analyses are retained, report the full list of genes used, the statistical significance of enrichment, the STRING confidence scores, and clearly label these as predictive, not experimental, findings. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Manuscript structure and clarity Claim pointer The manuscript contains duplicated text and structural inconsistencies. Evidence pointer Introduction section, Discussion section Concern The manuscript contains two Introduction sections, with the second one repeating content from the first. The Discussion section also contains duplicated paragraphs, with the same text appearing twice verbatim. This suggests a lack of careful editing and detracts from the readability and professionalism of the manuscript. Why it matters Duplicated text and structural errors undermine the credibility of the work and suggest that the manuscript has not been carefully prepared. Resolution test Remove duplicated sections and ensure a single, coherent Introduction and Discussion. Carefully proofread the entire manuscript for similar issues. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Title and abstract Evidence pointer Title, Abstract Issue The title states that mitochondria "affect antibacterial immunity in cross talk with innate immune response molecules coded by genes of nuclear origin." This phrasing implies a bidirectional interaction that is not demonstrated. The abstract similarly overstates the findings. Required correction Revise the title and abstract to reflect the descriptive and correlative nature of the study, e.g., "Differential expression of mitochondrial and nuclear-encoded immune genes in ducks during Pasteurella multocida infection" or similar. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Data availability Affected element Data availability statement Evidence pointer Data availability statement Issue The data availability statement is vague and does not specify which datasets are available or where they can be accessed. The accession numbers for the sequences are mentioned but not listed. Required correction Provide specific accession numbers for all submitted sequences and clarify which datasets are available in which repositories. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Figure quality Affected element Figures 1-14 Evidence pointer Figures 1-14 Issue The figures are not provided in the manuscript text, so their quality and clarity cannot be assessed. The figure legends are also not included. Required correction Ensure all figures and legends are included and that they clearly present the data with appropriate labels, scales, and statistical annotations. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Reference accuracy Affected element Reference list Evidence pointer Reference list Issue Some references appear to be cited in a format inconsistent with the journal style, and the completeness of the reference list cannot be verified. Required correction Verify all citations against the reference list and ensure formatting is consistent with the journal's requirements. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Language and grammar Affected element Entire manuscript Evidence pointer Entire manuscript Issue The manuscript contains numerous grammatical errors, awkward phrasings, and typographical issues that impede readability. Required correction The manuscript should be carefully edited by a native English speaker or professional editing service. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (no functional evidence for interaction), R1-M2 (inadequate statistical reporting), R1-M3 (incomplete methodological details) Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The topic of mitochondrial-nuclear cross talk in antibacterial immunity is of interest, but the approach is not novel methodologically, and the findings are largely descriptive. Scientific importance: The potential importance is moderate, but the lack of mechanistic insight limits the significance. Interdisciplinary readership: The work may appeal to immunologists, mitochondrial biologists, and veterinary scientists, but the narrow scope and descriptive nature limit broader appeal. Technical soundness: The in silico and expression methods are standard, but the statistical reporting and lack of functional validation are significant weaknesses. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is difficult to follow due to structural issues, duplicated text, and unclear writing. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript requires major revisions, including functional validation of the claimed interactions, rigorous statistical reporting, complete methodological details, and substantial rewriting to address structural and clarity issues, before the case can be considered. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of "first evidence" of mitochondrial-nuclear cross talk in duck pasteurellosis is unsupported, as no functional interaction is demonstrated. The claim that differential expression of cytochrome b and cytochrome c indicates enhanced mitochondrial activity or copy number is speculative and not directly measured. The pathway enrichment and STRING interaction claims are based on a very small gene set and are not statistically robust. The statement that "mitochondrial retrograde signalling influences the regulation of nuclear immune genes" is not supported by any experimental evidence. The conclusion that these genes "may serve as potential biomarkers" is speculative and not validated.

Assessment boundary Claims and methods as presented in the abstract; no figures, tables, or supplementary material were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report an integrated computational workflow combining deep learning-based virtual screening and molecular dynamics simulations to identify four structurally distinct FXIIa inhibitors (DR1-DR4) from a library of approximately 21 million compounds. They claim stable binding for all four compounds, more favorable binding free energies for DR1 and DR3 relative to a reference inhibitor, and favorable predicted pharmacokinetic properties. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, structural data, or validation experiments are visible Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, docking scores, binding free energy values, simulation convergence metrics, compound structures, and any experimental validation data Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a computationally intensive and methodologically reasonable workflow for identifying potential FXIIa inhibitors. The combination of deep learning-based docking tools with microsecond-scale molecular dynamics and binding free energy calculations is appropriate for the stated challenge of active-site flexibility. However, the abstract provides no quantitative results, no comparison metrics, and no experimental validation. The core claims of "stable binding" and "more favorable binding free energies" cannot be assessed without numerical data and statistical analysis. The work is potentially of interest to the anticoagulant discovery community, but the evidence presented in the abstract is insufficient to establish the case. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in thrombosis and hemostasis, medicinal chemists targeting coagulation factors, and computational chemists developing or applying deep learning-based virtual screening workflows. The potential for reduced bleeding risk anticoagulants is clinically relevant, and the methodological approach may interest those working on flexible active site targets. Major strengths The workflow addresses a recognized challenge in FXIIa inhibitor discovery, namely active-site flexibility, by using ensemble-based screening with microsecond-scale simulations. The use of multiple docking and rescoring tools in a hierarchical manner is a sound strategy. The library scale of approximately 21 million compounds is substantial and appropriate for a high-throughput virtual screen. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer "Microsecond-scale molecular dynamics simulations suggested stable binding of all four compounds to FXIIa, and binding free energy calculations suggested that DR1 and DR3 exhibited more favorable binding free energies than the reference inhibitor 1303." Evidence pointer Abstract, results section not provided Concern The claim of stable binding is based on simulations, but no quantitative metrics are provided, such as root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF), or interaction energy values. Similarly, the binding free energy comparison with the reference inhibitor is stated without any numerical values, error estimates, or statistical significance testing. The abstract does not indicate how many replicates were used for the binding free energy calculations or whether the differences are within the expected error of the MM/GBSA method. Why it matters Without quantitative data, the reader cannot determine whether the observed binding stability is meaningful or whether the free energy differences are statistically significant. MM/GBSA methods are known to have substantial error, and claims of superiority over a reference compound require error bars and replicate analysis. This is the central claim of the paper and cannot be evaluated from the abstract alone. Resolution test Provide RMSD and RMSF plots for all four compounds and the reference, binding free energy values with standard deviations from multiple independent simulations, and a statistical test (e.g., t-test or bootstrap) comparing DR1 and DR3 to the reference inhibitor. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Validation Claim pointer "Four structurally distinct hits (DR1-DR4) were identified." Evidence pointer Abstract, results section not provided Concern The abstract reports identification of four hits from a virtual screen but provides no experimental validation, no orthogonal computational validation beyond the same docking/scoring family, and no comparison to known FXIIa inhibitors other than the single reference compound. The abstract does not state whether these compounds were tested in any biochemical or cellular assay. Why it matters Virtual screening hits frequently fail in experimental assays due to false positives, solubility issues, or off-target effects. Without any experimental validation, the claim that these are "hits" is premature. The term "hit" implies some level of confirmed activity, which is not demonstrated. Resolution test Provide experimental IC50 or Ki values for DR1-DR4 against FXIIa, or clearly rephrase the claim to "computationally predicted candidates" and add a statement that experimental validation is ongoing or planned. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Methodological transparency Claim pointer "A hierarchical screening workflow was carried out in DrugFlow using KarmaDock for primary screening, CarsiDock for redocking, and RTMScore for rescoring." Evidence pointer Abstract, methods section not provided Concern The abstract does not specify the scoring thresholds, the number of compounds retained at each stage, or the criteria for selecting the final four hits. The enrichment rate from 21 million to 4 compounds is not described, and no performance metrics for the docking tools on this specific target are provided. Why it matters Without knowing the selection criteria and the attrition at each stage, the reader cannot assess whether the workflow is reproducible or whether the final hits are the result of a reasonable filtering process. The lack of thresholds makes it impossible to evaluate the stringency of the screen. Resolution test Provide a flowchart or table showing the number of compounds at each stage, the scoring cutoffs used, and the rationale for the final selection. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Methods description Evidence pointer Abstract, methods section Issue The abstract states that "missing regions were modeled with MODELLER" but does not specify which regions of the FXIIa catalytic domain were missing or the confidence in the modeled structure. Required correction Specify the missing residues and provide a validation metric for the modeled regions, such as a Ramachandran plot or DOPE score. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Pharmacokinetic claims Evidence pointer Abstract, results section Issue The claim of "favorable predicted pharmacokinetic properties" is vague. The abstract does not state which properties were predicted (e.g., solubility, permeability, metabolic stability) or the specific values. Required correction List the specific pharmacokinetic parameters predicted and provide the values for each compound, with a brief comparison to the reference inhibitor. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Simulation details Evidence pointer Abstract, methods section Issue The abstract does not specify the number of replicates for the binding free energy calculations or the length of the production runs used for the MMPBSA analysis. Required correction State the number of independent simulations and the trajectory length used for the binding free energy calculations. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (lack of quantitative binding data and statistical analysis), R1-M2 (no experimental validation or clear rephrasing of the "hit" claim), R1-M3 (missing screening thresholds and attrition data) Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The application of deep learning-based docking to FXIIa with ensemble-based screening is moderately original, though similar workflows have been reported for other targets. Scientific importance: The potential for safer anticoagulants is clinically significant, but the abstract does not demonstrate that the identified compounds have any functional activity. Interdisciplinary readership: The work bridges computational chemistry and thrombosis research, which could attract a broad audience if the results are robust. Technical soundness: The methods are appropriate in principle, but the lack of quantitative results and validation prevents assessment of technical execution. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is generally clear, though the deep learning tool names and simulation details may be opaque to non-computational readers. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The workflow is reasonable and the target is clinically relevant, but the abstract lacks the quantitative data and validation needed to support the central claims. I would be supportive if the full manuscript provides binding free energy values with error analysis, simulation stability metrics, and at least preliminary experimental validation or a clear statement that these are computational predictions pending experimental testing. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that DR1 and DR3 exhibit "more favorable binding free energies" than the reference inhibitor is unsupported without numerical values and statistical analysis. The claim of "stable binding" for all four compounds is unsupported without RMSD/RMSF data or interaction energy analysis. The characterization of DR1-DR4 as "hits" is unsupported without experimental activity data. The claim of "favorable predicted pharmacokinetic properties" is unverifiable without specific parameters and values. The overall implication that these compounds are viable leads for anticoagulant discovery is premature without experimental validation.

or statistical analyses Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report a cryo-EM structure of the NPC1-NPC2 complex at lysosomal pH with a bis-sterol ligand, showing an expanded neck conformation with no sterol in the central tunnel. They propose that cholesterol occupancy, not pH, controls tunnel contraction, and integrate structures with MD simulations to propose a substrate-induced gating cycle resembling alternating access. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, methods, or supplementary materials provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, structural statistics, MD simulation parameters, validation metrics, and all figures/tables Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially significant structural finding and a conceptual model for NPC1-mediated cholesterol transport. The claim that cholesterol occupancy rather than pH governs tunnel conformation is testable and interesting. However, the evidence base visible here is insufficient to evaluate the rigor of the structural assignments, the MD simulation methodology, or the strength of the proposed gating model. The conceptual leap from static structures and simulations to a full alternating access mechanism requires more direct experimental support than is visible in the abstract. Who would be interested in the results, and why Structural biologists studying membrane proteins and transport mechanisms; researchers in the lysosomal storage disease field, particularly those working on Niemann-Pick disease type C; computational biologists interested in lipid transport simulations; and pharmaceutical scientists targeting NPC1 for therapeutic intervention. Major strengths The work addresses a long-standing mechanistic gap in NPC1-mediated cholesterol transport. The use of a bis-sterol ligand to stabilize a functional complex is an innovative approach. The proposal that substrate occupancy rather than pH controls conformational state is a clear, falsifiable hypothesis. The integration of structural and computational approaches is appropriate for the question. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The claim that cholesterol occupancy in the neck site is a key determinant of tunnel contraction Evidence pointer Abstract, location not provided Concern The abstract states that NPC1 purified from cholesterol-auxotrophic insect cells exhibits an expanded neck conformation, which is used to support the occupancy model. However, the abstract does not report whether this expanded conformation was observed in the presence or absence of the bis-sterol ligand, nor does it describe any direct manipulation of cholesterol occupancy to demonstrate causality. The comparison between the ligand-bound complex and the cholesterol-depleted protein is suggestive but does not establish that occupancy is the causal determinant. Why it matters The central mechanistic claim of the paper rests on this causal relationship. Without direct evidence that varying cholesterol occupancy alone produces the observed conformational change, the conclusion is correlative rather than causal. Resolution test Provide experiments where cholesterol occupancy is varied independently of pH and ligand presence, with clear structural readouts. Alternatively, show that the expanded conformation is reversed upon cholesterol addition to the purified protein. 01 基本信息 标题 ：TurboPairFormer: Fast and Stable Protein Folding Model Training with an Optimized Triangle Attention Kernel 作者 ：Yide Ran; Chelsea Lowman; Jan Domański; David Hartmann; Jenke Scheen; Jennifer Wei; Chuan Li; Jianwen Xie; Zhaozhuo Xu 单位 ：未提供（arXiv 页面未列出作者单位） 期刊/平台 ：arXiv 预印本 年份 ：2026（提交日期 2026-10-05） 论文类型 ：预印本（方法/系统论文） 领域 ：CS > Machine Learning；蛋白质结构预测模型训练加速 关键词 ：Triangle Attention、Kernel 优化、蛋白质折叠、训练稳定性、GPU 加速 DOI/arXiv 号 ：arXiv:2610.05854v1 代码 ：未提供 数据 ：未提供 阅读日期 ：2026-10-05 在该方向中的位置 ：本文聚焦于蛋白质结构预测模型（如 AlphaFold 类架构）中 triangle attention 算子的 GPU kernel 级优化，属于「蛋白质结构相关计算研究 × AI 方法」中的 训练基础设施/算子优化 子方向，与模型架构创新（如 Evoformer 变体）和物理模拟（MD/对接）正交，但直接服务于大规模结构预测模型的训练效率与稳定性。 02 一句话总结 本文通过重新设计 triangle attention 的 GPU kernel 实现（优化内存访问模式与并行策略），在不改变模型数学语义的前提下，显著加速蛋白质折叠模型的训练并提升训练稳定性，实验表明在保持精度的同时训练速度提升且损失曲线更平滑。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：AlphaFold 类蛋白质结构预测模型中的 triangle attention 算子在 GPU 上计算效率低、内存占用高，导致训练速度慢且训练过程不稳定（如损失震荡、梯度爆炸）。 为什么重要 ：蛋白质结构预测模型的训练成本极高（AlphaFold2 训练需数百 GPU 天），triangle attention 是其中计算密集的核心算子之一；提升其效率可直接降低训练门槛，使更大规模模型或更长训练成为可能。 现有方法为何不足 ：现有 kernel 实现（如 JAX/FLAX 默认实现或 PyTorch 原生实现）未针对 triangle attention 的稀疏三角结构做专门优化，存在大量冗余计算和低效内存访问；同时数值稳定性处理不足，导致训练中梯度异常。 精确研究问题 ：Can a custom GPU kernel for triangle attention, designed with optimized memory access and numerical stabilization, achieve faster and more stable training of protein folding models without altering model accuracy? point (pI) that combines optimized pKa values for seven ionizable residue types and two termini with embeddings from a pretrained protein language model. 01 基本信息 标题 : Capturing Hu Antigen R Domain Closure Through Supervised Molecular Dynamics Simulations 作者与单位 : Cavastracci Strascia, Chiara; Dodaro, Andrea; Novello, Gianluca; Menin, Silvia; Sturlese, Mattia; Salmaso, Veronica; Moro, Stefano（意大利帕多瓦大学，Università degli Studi di Padova） 期刊/预印本平台 : ChemMedChem 年份 : 2026（在线日期 2026-10-05） 论文类型 : 研究论文（方法应用 + 机制研究） 领域 : 蛋白质构象转变的增强采样模拟；RNA 结合蛋白；药物发现 关键词 : HuR；Supervised MD (SuMD)；构象转变；RRM 结构域；RNA 结合；分子动力学 DOI/arXiv 号 : 10.1002/cmdc.70523 代码 : https://github.com/molecularmodelingsection/SuMD（SuMD 代码，免费可用） 数据 : 未提供（PDB 结构 4EGL 和 4ED5 为输入） 阅读日期 : 2026-05-14（模拟日期） 在课题方向中的位置 : 本文属于「蛋白质构象采样 × 物理模拟（MD）」方向，将原本用于分子间识别（配体-靶标、蛋白-核酸）的 SuMD 方法首次拓展至 分子内结构域闭合 这一构象转变问题，为蛋白质构象采样提供了新的增强采样思路，并直接服务于 RNA 结合蛋白的变构/口袋发现。 02 一句话总结 针对 HuR 蛋白 RRM1-RRM2 串联结构域从开放（apo）到闭合（RNA 结合）的构象转变，作者开发了基于残基对距离监督的多步 SuMD 协议，成功在纳秒时间尺度上重现了近晶体结构的闭合构象（RRM2 骨架 RMSD ≈ 9 Å），并揭示了 linker 区 Arg97 在闭合过程中的关键驱动作用。 03 研究问题 具体问题 : HuR 蛋白的 RRM1-RRM2 串联结构域如何从 apo 开放构象转变为 RNA 结合的闭合构象？能否用增强采样 MD 方法在可行计算成本内重现这一分子内构象转变？ 为什么重要 : HuR 是癌症、炎症和神经退行性疾病中的潜在药物靶点，但其 RNA 结合界面大且高度溶剂暴露、构象灵活，缺乏适合小分子结合的明确口袋。理解其开放-闭合转变机制有助于识别瞬时口袋，指导靶向 HuR 的药物设计。 现有方法为何不足 : 常规 MD 模拟（3×500 ns）无法在微秒以下时间尺度捕获开放-闭合转变（apo 模拟中仅瞬态接近闭合构象，RMSD 最低 7.88 Å 但仅维持数帧）；单步 SuMD 监督（监督两个结构域界面的质心距离）也不足以驱动完整的构象重排。 精确研究问题 : Can a multistep SuMD protocol, supervising selected interdomain residue pairs, reproduce the open-to-closed domain closure of HuR within nanosecond timescales and identify key residues driving this transition? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：以下脉络主要基于本文框架，部分经外部核验（标注）。 HuR 结构与功能研究 （外部核验）: HuR 含三个 RRM 结构域，RRM1-RRM2 串联负责 RNA 结合。PDB 中已有 apo（4EGL）和 RNA 结合（4ED5）两种构象，二者差异显著——RRM2 相对 RRM1 旋转约 180°。Wang et al. [1] 通过丙氨酸扫描鉴定 Arg97、Arg136、Arg147 为关键 RNA 结合残基。 MD 模拟在蛋白质构象转变中的应用 （本文框架）: 常规 MD 受限于采样时间尺度，难以捕获大尺度构象重排；增强采样方法（如 metadynamics、replica exchange）虽可加速采样，但往往需要预先定义集体变量或大量计算资源。 SuMD 方法的发展 （外部核验）: SuMD 由 Moro 课题组开发，最初用于配体-靶标结合路径模拟 [23-28]，通过短 MD 片段的监督筛选（监督分子间质心距离的下降趋势）显著加速结合事件采样。近期被拓展至蛋白-核酸识别（含无序蛋白）[22]。 本文位置 : 首次将 SuMD 从分子间识别拓展至 分子内结构域闭合 ，并引入「多步监督」策略（先监督 linker-RRM2 残基对，再监督跨结构域残基对），解决了单步监督无法驱动完整构象转变的问题。 05 核心痛点 痛点 表现 成因或作者解释 文中证据 常规 MD 无法采样开放→闭合转变 3×500 ns apo MD 中 RRM2 RMSD 平均 33 Å，仅一次瞬态接近闭合（7.88 Å，数帧） 构象转变涉及 linker 旋转和结构域重排，能垒高、时间尺度远超常规 MD 可达范围 Results 图 2A-B、图 S3、表 1 单步 SuMD 监督不足 监督 RRM1/RRM2 RNA 结合界面质心距离的 4 次 SuMD 均失败（RMSD > 44 Å） 质心距离监督过于粗糙，无法引导 linker 旋转和结构域相对取向的精确调整 Results 第 2 节、图 S4 缺乏区分成功/失败 SuMD 轨迹的指标 仅凭 RMSD 判断轨迹质量，但 RMSD 高时可能仍存在局部正确相互作用 需要结合相互作用能、残基接触等多维度评估 Results 表 2、表 3、图 S5-S6 瞬时口袋难以捕捉 闭合过程中可能暴露瞬时口袋，但终点构象（apo/闭合）中不可见 构象转变路径上的中间态可能具有独特口袋特征 Results 图 7、Conclusions 06 核心思想 表面方法 : 采用多步 SuMD 协议——第一步监督 linker 区残基 Ile103 与 RRM2 残基 Lys156 的距离（促进 linker 旋转），第二步监督 RRM1 残基 Lys92 与 RRM2 残基 Asn134 的距离（促进结构域闭合）。每步 4 次独立 SuMD 运行，从 apo 构象出发，在 RNA 存在下模拟闭合。 核心洞察 : - 分子内构象转变的监督变量应选择 在开放/闭合两态间距离变化最大且位于关键运动节点（如 linker）的残基对 ，而非简单的结构域质心距离。 - 多步监督（先局部后全局）比单步监督更有效，因为构象转变存在层级性——linker 旋转是结构域闭合的前提。 - 闭合路径中 linker 残基 Arg97 的侧链重取向（从朝外到朝内）是驱动闭合的关键事件，与突变数据一致。 [Analysis] 可能的普适教训 : 对于任何涉及结构域重排的蛋白质构象转变（如激酶激活、转录因子 DNA 结合），SuMD 的监督变量设计应遵循「先识别两态间位移最大的残基对，再按运动层级分步监督」的原则。这一思路可迁移至其他柔性多结构域蛋白的构象采样问题。 07 方法总览 输入 : apo 构象（PDB 4EGL，开放态） RNA 结合构象（PDB 4ED5，闭合态，用于定义目标残基对距离） RNA 分子（来自 4ED5，放置在 RRM1 结合界面） 输出 : 闭合轨迹（近晶体构象，RRM2 RMSD ≈ 9 Å） 闭合路径上的关键残基/相互作用 瞬时口袋候选 模块 : 1. 结构准备（MOE）：序列校正、缺失残基构建、加氢、质子化（pH 7.4）、linker 区（Arg97-Gly102）建模 2. 体系搭建（AmberTools22）：TIP3P 水盒子（20 Å 等距）、0.154 M NaCl、Amber14SB（蛋白）+ OL3（RNA）力场 3. 平衡（ACEMD 3.5）：两步平衡（NVT 1 ns + NPT 1 ns，5 kcal/mol·Å² restraints） 4. 常规 MD：3×500 ns（apo、闭合、pseudo-apo） 5. No figures, tables, or supplementary materials were provided for inspection. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the textual content of the manuscript. Claims regarding simulation results, structural analyses, and methodological outcomes are evaluated based on the descriptions provided in the text alone. No raw data, trajectory files, or structural coordinates were available for independent verification. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report that (i) conventional MD simulations of the apo HuR tandem RRM1-RRM2 construct show extensive interdomain motions while the RNA-bound complex remains stable; (ii) a novel application of Supervised MD (SuMD) to an intramolecular conformational transition, using a multistep supervision protocol based on selected interdomain residue pairs, reproduces a closed conformation resembling the experimental RNA-bound structure; (iii) per-residue interaction analyses identify key contributions from the linker region, particularly Arg97, Arg136, and Arg147, consistent with published mutagenesis data; and (iv) the reclosure pathway transiently exposes putative druggable pockets not detectable in endpoint conformations. Visible evidence base Textual descriptions of simulation protocols, RMSD and RMSF values, interaction energy analyses, residue-level contact patterns, and pocket detection results. Specific numerical values are reported for some quantities (e.g., RMSD values of 9.04 Å, 4.33 Å, 14.57 Å; interaction energy of −560.60 kcal/mol), but the corresponding figures, tables, and supplementary materials are not available for inspection. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures (Figures 1-7), tables (Tables 1-3, S1, S2), supplementary figures (Figures S1-S10), and Video S1 were not provided. These materials are essential for evaluating the validity of the reported structural analyses, the quality of the SuMD trajectories, the convergence assessments, and the pocket detection results. Without these, several key claims cannot be independently verified. Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript presents a methodologically interesting application of SuMD to an intramolecular conformational transition in HuR, a target of therapeutic relevance. The authors are transparent about the limitations of their approach, including the stochastic nature of SuMD and the lack of a validated metric to distinguish productive from unproductive trajectories. However, the manuscript has several significant weaknesses that currently prevent a full endorsement. The central claim of reproducing a "closed conformation resembling the experimental RNA-bound structure" rests on a single successful trajectory out of multiple attempts, and the reported RMSD values (9.04 Å for the full construct) are high by structural biology standards. The mechanistic interpretation, while plausible, is derived from a single trajectory and lacks statistical support. The pocket detection analysis is explicitly preliminary and the authors appropriately caution against overinterpretation, but the inclusion of this material without more rigorous validation adds limited value. The manuscript would benefit from a more critical discussion of what constitutes "success" in this context, additional validation of the SuMD-derived pathway, and a clearer articulation of the practical utility of the identified transient pockets. The writing is generally clear, though some methodological details require clarification. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational chemists and biophysicists working on enhanced sampling methods, particularly those interested in extending SuMD-type approaches beyond intermolecular recognition to intramolecular conformational transitions. Researchers studying RNA-binding proteins, especially HuR, as a therapeutic target in oncology and neurodegeneration, may find the mechanistic insights into domain closure and the identification of transient pockets of interest for structure-based drug design efforts. Methodologists developing supervised or directed sampling techniques would also be interested in the multistep supervision protocol described here. Major strengths (1) The manuscript addresses a biologically and therapeutically relevant question: the conformational transition of HuR between open and closed states, which is central to its RNA-binding function. (2) The extension of SuMD to an intramolecular transition is a novel methodological contribution, and the authors are appropriately cautious in framing this as a first application. (3) The multistep supervision protocol, inspired by prior work on protein-nucleic acid recognition, is a thoughtful adaptation that addresses the failure of single-step supervision. (4) The authors are transparent about the limitations of their approach, including the stochastic nature of SuMD, the lack of a validated success metric, and the preliminary nature of the pocket analysis. (5) The per-residue interaction analysis recovers experimentally validated key residues (Arg97, Arg136, Arg147), providing some confidence in the biological relevance of the simulated pathway. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness / Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The authors claim that the multistep SuMD protocol "succeeded in reproducing a nearly crystal-like conformation of closed RNA-bound HuR, with an RMSD of 9.04 Å for the RRM2 backbone." Evidence pointer Results and Discussion, "Simulations of HuR Conformational Transition" section; Figure 5; Figure S7; location not provided for specific figure panels Concern The central success claim rests on a single trajectory (run1 of Supervision Step-2) out of four attempts. An RMSD of 9.04 Å for the RRM2 backbone relative to the crystal structure is substantial and does not constitute a "nearly crystal-like" conformation by conventional structural biology standards. The authors note that when aligning on the entire backbone the RMSD drops to 4.33 Å, but this is a global measure that may mask local structural deviations. The manuscript does not report whether the key interdomain contacts, hydrogen bonds, and salt bridges observed in the crystal structure are faithfully reproduced in the SuMD-derived closed state. Without a residue-level comparison of the simulated closed state to the experimental structure, the claim of "reproducing" the closed conformation is not adequately supported. Furthermore, the persistence assessment is based on a single 100 ns unbiased MD simulation, which is too short to establish stability. Why it matters The entire methodological contribution hinges on the ability of the multistep SuMD protocol to generate a conformation that is meaningfully similar to the experimentally determined closed state. If the 9.04 Å RMSD reflects a conformation that is only superficially similar to the crystal structure, with incorrect interdomain contacts or an improperly formed RNA-binding cleft, then the claimed success is overstated and the mechanistic interpretations derived from this trajectory are unreliable. Resolution test The authors should provide a detailed residue-level comparison between the SuMD-generated closed state and the crystal structure, including: (a) a per-residue RMSD plot with the secondary structure elements annotated; (b) a contact map comparison highlighting which native interdomain contacts are reproduced and which are not; (c) an analysis of the RNA-binding cleft geometry (e.g., width, depth, electrostatic potential) in the simulated closed state versus the crystal structure; and (d) a longer persistence simulation (at least 500 ns, ideally multiple replicates) demonstrating that the closed state is stable. If the simulated closed state deviates significantly from the crystal structure in functionally important regions, the claims should be revised accordingly. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness / Methodological rigor Claim pointer The authors state that "the identified pathway should be regarded as one plausible route among potentially multiple closure mechanisms" and that the per-residue interaction analysis "recovered several residues previously reported in the literature as key residues for RNA recognition." Evidence pointer Results and Discussion, "Simulations of HuR Conformational Transition" section; Figure 6; location not provided for specific figure panels Concern The mechanistic interpretation of the reclosure pathway is derived from a single successful trajectory. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the conclusions, but the Results section presents the pathway and the residue-level interactions as if they are robust findings. The per-residue interaction energy analysis is performed on one trajectory, and no error bars, replicate analyses, or statistical measures are reported. The claim that the analysis "confirmed the prominent role of Arg97" is based on a single simulation and cannot be considered a confirmation in any meaningful sense. Additionally, the selection of the "most productive" trajectory for further analysis introduces a selection bias that is not addressed. Why it matters The mechanistic insights into HuR domain closure are presented as a key outcome of the study. If these insights are derived from a single stochastic trajectory, they may not be reproducible or representative of the ensemble of possible closure pathways. The authors' own acknowledgment that SuMD is stochastic and that different initial velocities can lead to markedly different trajectories undermines the confidence that can be placed in the specific pathway and residue interactions described. Resolution test The authors should either (a) demonstrate that the key mechanistic features (e.g., the role of Arg97, the sequence of interdomain contact formation) are reproducible across multiple independent SuMD runs that yield productive closure, or (b) explicitly reframe the findings as observations from a single trajectory that require experimental validation, with appropriate caveats throughout the Results section rather than only in the Conclusions. If multiple productive trajectories are available, a statistical analysis of the conserved versus variable features of the closure pathway should be provided. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Scientific importance / Translational relevance Claim pointer The authors state that "the pool of the collected trajectories also revealed novel conformational states accessible to the protein, which may represent valuable structural templates for future computer-aided drug design studies and for the identification of transiently druggable conformational states." Evidence pointer Results and Discussion, "Simulations of HuR Conformational Transition" section; Figure 7; location not provided for specific figure panels Concern The pocket detection analysis is explicitly preliminary, and the authors appropriately note that the druggability score is a geometric and physicochemical estimator, not a demonstration of genuine druggability. However, the claim that these pockets "may represent valuable structural templates" is speculative and not supported by any functional validation. The manuscript does not assess whether the identified pockets could accommodate drug-like molecules in a manner that would disrupt HuR-RNA interactions, nor does it compare these pockets to known small-molecule binding sites on HuR. The inclusion of this analysis without more rigorous validation (e.g., molecular docking of known HuR ligands, comparison to experimental binding data) weakens the translational claims. Why it matters The potential for targeting transient conformational states of HuR is a significant motivation for this work. If the identified pockets are artifacts of the simulation protocol or are not functionally relevant, the translational value of the study is diminished. Overstating the significance of preliminary computational predictions could mislead future drug discovery efforts. Resolution test The authors should either (a) provide additional computational validation, such as docking known HuR ligands or drug-like fragments into the identified pockets and assessing their predicted binding affinities, or (b) temper the claims about the translational value of the pockets, explicitly stating that these are preliminary observations requiring experimental validation. If the pockets are not conserved across multiple trajectories or are not stable in longer simulations, this should be reported. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity / Reproducibility Affected element Methods, "SuMD" section Evidence pointer Materials and Methods, "SuMD" section; location not provided Issue The description of the SuMD supervision protocol lacks specific details on how the "distance between the centers of mass" was computed for residue pairs. It is unclear whether this refers to the distance between the Cα atoms, the side-chain centroids, or the centers of mass of the entire residues. Additionally, the criteria for accepting or rejecting a SuMD step are described only in terms of the slope of the fitted line, but the specific threshold values and the length of each SuMD step are not clearly stated. Required correction Provide a precise definition of the distance metric used for supervision, including the atoms or groups considered. Specify the exact acceptance criteria for SuMD steps (e.g., the slope threshold) and the duration of each SuMD step in simulation time. This information is essential for reproducibility. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Clarity / Data presentation Affected element Results and Discussion, "MD Simulations of HuR in the Open and Closed Conformation" section Evidence pointer Results and Discussion, "MD Simulations of HuR in the Open and Closed Conformation" section; Table 1; location not provided Issue The manuscript reports average RMSD values for the apo and RNA-bound systems (e.g., 33.00 Å and 2.65 Å, respectively) but does not provide standard deviations or ranges across the three replicates. The text states that the apo form "displayed extensive interdomain motions," but without a measure of variability, it is difficult to assess the consistency of this observation across replicates. Required correction Report the standard deviation or range for the average RMSD values across replicates. Consider showing the RMSD time series for each replicate in the supplementary materials to allow readers to assess the variability and convergence of the simulations. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Clarity / Terminology Affected element Results and Discussion, "Simulations of HuR Conformational Transition" section Evidence pointer Results and Discussion, "Simulations of HuR Conformational Transition" section; location not provided Issue The term "Supervision Step-1" and "Supervision Step-2" is used to describe the two stages of the multistep protocol, but the relationship between these steps and the earlier "Case 1" and "Case 2" designations is not immediately clear. The text states that Case 1 and Case 2 were "described above as Supervision Step-1," but this connection could be made more explicit. Required correction Use consistent terminology throughout the manuscript. Either refer to the two cases as "Supervision Step-1 (Case 1)" and "Supervision Step-1 (Case 2)" throughout, or introduce a clear mapping between the two naming schemes at the first mention. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Completeness / Data availability Affected element Results and Discussion, "Simulations of HuR Conformational Transition" section Evidence pointer Results and Discussion, "Simulations of HuR Conformational Transition" section; Figure S9; Figure S10; location not provided Issue The manuscript mentions that a panel of images showing the last frame of all SuMD trajectories is provided in Figures S9 and S10, but the criteria for classifying trajectories as "Productive" versus "Unproductive" are not explicitly defined. The text implies that productivity is related to the final RMSD and interaction energy, but the specific thresholds are not stated. Required correction Define the criteria used to classify trajectories as productive or unproductive. If the classification is based on RMSD or interaction energy thresholds, specify these values. If the classification is qualitative, state this explicitly. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established (1) The central claim of reproducing the closed conformation is based on a single trajectory with a high RMSD (9.04 Å) that is not rigorously compared to the crystal structure at the residue level. (2) The mechanistic interpretations are derived from one trajectory without statistical support or replicate analysis. (3) The pocket detection analysis is preliminary and lacks validation of functional relevance. (4) The manuscript does not provide sufficient details on the SuMD supervision protocol for reproducibility. (5) The persistence assessment is based on a single short (100 ns) simulation, which is insufficient to establish stability. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The application of SuMD to an intramolecular conformational transition is a novel methodological contribution. While the approach is an incremental extension of existing SuMD methodology, the specific application to HuR domain closure has not been previously reported. Scientific importance: The study addresses a biologically relevant question with therapeutic implications, but the significance of the findings is limited by the preliminary nature of the results and the lack of experimental validation. The mechanistic insights, while plausible, are derived from a single trajectory and require further support. Interdisciplinary readership: The manuscript is likely to appeal primarily to computational chemists and biophysicists specializing in enhanced sampling methods. The broader structural biology and drug discovery communities may find the results of interest, but the technical nature of the study limits its accessibility. Technical soundness: The simulation protocols are generally sound, and the authors demonstrate awareness of methodological limitations. However, the lack of statistical rigor in the analysis of the single successful trajectory and the insufficient validation of the claimed "nearly crystal-like" conformation are significant technical weaknesses. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is clearly written and the authors make an effort to explain the SuMD methodology. However, the results section assumes familiarity with molecular dynamics simulation techniques and structural analysis methods, which may limit accessibility for readers outside the computational biophysics community. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The manuscript presents a novel methodological application with potential value for the computational biophysics community. However, the central claims require substantial additional analysis and validation before they can be fully endorsed. Specifically, the authors must provide a rigorous residue-level comparison of the SuMD-generated closed state to the crystal structure, demonstrate reproducibility of the key mechanistic findings across multiple trajectories, and either strengthen or temper the claims regarding druggable pockets. The manuscript would also benefit from a more critical discussion of what constitutes "success" in reproducing a conformational transition and the limitations of using a single trajectory for mechanistic interpretation. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the multistep SuMD protocol "succeeded in reproducing a nearly crystal-like conformation" is not fully supported by the reported RMSD value of 9.04 Å, which is high by structural biology standards, and the lack of a residue-level comparison to the crystal structure. The claim that the per-residue interaction analysis "confirmed" the role of Arg97, Arg136, and Arg147 is unsupported, as the analysis is based on a single trajectory and no statistical measures are provided. The claim that the identified pockets "may represent valuable structural templates for future computer-aided drug design studies" is speculative and not supported by any functional validation or comparison to known HuR ligand binding data. The statement that the closed state "persisted without undergoing a major reopening" during the 100 ns unbiased MD simulation is based on a single short simulation and cannot be considered evidence of stability. The claim that the identified pathway is "a plausible reclosure pathway" is reasonable as a hypothesis, but the manuscript does not provide sufficient evidence to distinguish this pathway from other possible mechanisms.

01 基本信息 标题 ：D-DOIT: Training-free Adaptation of Discrete Diffusion via Doob's h-Transform 作者 ：Jieke Wu; Qijie Zhu; Weimin Wu; Zeqi Ye; Minshuo Chen; Han Liu 单位 ：未提供 期刊/预印本平台 ：arXiv（预印本） 年份 ：2026（提交日期 2026-10-04） 论文类型 ：方法论文（training-free adaptation 方法） 领域 ：Machine Learning（离散扩散模型） 关键词 ：discrete diffusion, Doob's h-transform, training-free adaptation, guided generation DOI/arXiv 号 ：arXiv:2610.04938v1 代码 ：未提供 数据 ：未提供 阅读日期 ：2026-05-12（当前日期） 该文在课题方向中的位置 ：本文属于生成模型方法研究，不直接涉及蛋白质结构。但其核心思想——通过 Doob's h-Transform 实现 training-free 的离散扩散模型条件化/引导——可迁移至蛋白质序列设计、离散残基采样、以及结构生成中的约束满足问题。对于蛋白质结构相关计算研究，本文提供了一种无需重新训练即可将任意约束（如结构 motif、功能位点）注入离散扩散采样过程的数学框架。 02 一句话总结 本文提出 D-DOIT 框架，利用 Doob's h-Transform 在离散扩散模型的采样过程中直接注入任意约束（以势函数形式给出），无需任何训练或微调，即可实现条件生成，并在多个离散生成任务上验证了其有效性。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：如何在不对离散扩散模型进行额外训练或微调的前提下，将任意约束（如属性条件、结构约束）注入到生成过程中？ 为什么重要 ：离散扩散模型在文本、图、蛋白质序列等离散数据生成中表现优异，但实际应用常需条件生成（如指定属性、满足约束）。现有方法（如 classifier guidance）需要训练额外的分类器或修改模型，成本高且不灵活。 现有方法为何不足 ：classifier guidance 需要训练分类器；classifier-free guidance 需要条件训练数据；其他 adaptation 方法（如微调）需要大量计算资源。这些方法均无法做到"即插即用"的约束注入。 精确研究问题 ：Can we perform training-free conditional generation with discrete diffusion models by directly modifying the sampling process via Doob's h-Transform, without any parameter updates? 本文提出一种在扩散模型推理阶段对生成生物分子结构施加物理有效性约束的投影方法，通过将生成样本投影到满足物理规则的流形上，在不重新训练模型的前提下提升生成结构的物理合理性。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：扩散模型在生成生物分子（如蛋白质）结构时，虽然能产生多样且接近天然构象的样本，但生成的结构常常违反基本的物理化学规则（如键长、键角、原子间距离、手性等），导致结构在物理上不可行。 为什么重要 ：物理无效的结构无法直接用于下游任务（如分子对接、MD 模拟、药物筛选），限制了生成模型在实际计算研究中的应用价值。 现有方法为何不足 ：现有方法多在训练阶段加入物理约束（如修改损失函数、引入辅助物理模块），但这样做需要重新训练模型，计算成本高且可能损害生成多样性；同时，训练时的约束难以覆盖所有物理规则，推理时仍可能出现违反。 精确研究问题 ：Can we enforce physical validity on biomolecular diffusion model outputs at inference time via projection, without retraining the generative model? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：此脉络基于本文框架及该领域公开常识构建，标注「经外部核验」部分。 阶段 代表性方法 优点 局限 本文位置 早期结构生成 扩散模型的去噪过程是逐步的，每一步的中间样本都处于「接近数据分布但可能物理无效」的状态。如果能在每一步将样本投影到物理可行空间，则最终生成的结构既保持数据分布特性，又满足物理规则。关键在于投影操作需要与扩散过程兼容，不能破坏去噪的收敛性。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] 推理时约束（inference-time hierarchical learning framework that first selects subgraph regions likely to contain minority nodes, then performs fine-grained node classification within those regions, effectively mitigate class The method first applies a coarse subgraph-level classifier to select regions likely to contain minority instances, then a fine-grained node-level predictor within those regions. no full text, figures, tables, or supplementary materials were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present GalaxyMemMD, an open-source Galaxy framework that integrates membrane embedding, system preparation, MD execution, and downstream analysis into a single reproducible pipeline. They claim high-throughput parallel simulation support across multiple membrane compositions and protein variants, compatibility with AlphaFold-derived structures and molecular docking workflows, and validation across six membrane proteins demonstrating consistent system preparation, stable embeddings, and reproducible trajectory-level production. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, benchmark details, or methodological descriptions are available Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, benchmark protocols, software documentation, code repository, and any statistical analyses Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a potentially valuable software contribution that addresses a real gap in membrane protein MD simulation workflows. The integration of embedding, simulation, and analysis within a Galaxy framework is a sensible and potentially impactful approach. However, the abstract provides insufficient technical detail and quantitative evidence to evaluate the core claims of reproducibility, scalability, and equivalence to established tools. The validation across six proteins is mentioned but not substantiated with any metrics or comparisons. The manuscript cannot be assessed for technical soundness from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biophysicists and structural biologists who use MD simulations to study membrane proteins would be the primary audience. Researchers seeking accessible, reproducible, and scalable simulation pipelines, particularly those without extensive HPC expertise, would benefit. The Galaxy community and developers of bioinformatics workflows may also find the integration approach of interest. The potential to incorporate AlphaFold structures and docking workflows broadens appeal to the structural biology community. Major strengths The proposed tool addresses a clear and important bottleneck in membrane protein simulation, namely the lack of a complete end-to-end pipeline. The use of Galaxy provides a well-established framework for reproducibility and accessibility. The claimed support for high-throughput parallel simulations across multiple membrane compositions and protein variants is a meaningful capability extension beyond existing preparation-only tools. The integration of modern structure prediction and docking frameworks is forward-looking.
